This is a ruling concerning one specific woman, so the verb is past tense. The reading with the kasrah is for the future, concerning every woman who would give herself, not one specific woman. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "idh wahabat" (when she gave herself). "Idh" is an adverb of past time, so it refers to a specific woman.

He turned from address (khiṭāb) to the third person (ghaybah) regarding the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿if the Prophet desires﴾, then returned to address in His words: ﴿exclusively for you﴾, to indicate that this is among what was specially granted to him and given preference. Its coming in the wording "the Prophet" indicates that the exclusivity is an honour for him on account of prophethood. Its repetition is a glorification of him and an affirmation that he deserves this honour because of his prophethood.

Istinkah means seeking to marry her and desiring it.

The majority hold that marriage is not valid with the wording of hire (ijarah) nor with the wording of gift (hibah). Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi said: it is valid with the wording of hire, based on His words: ﴿those whose bridal payments (ujur) you have given﴾. The argument of those who prohibit it is that a contract of hire is time-limited, while a marriage contract is permanent, so the two are contradictory.

Abu Hanifah and his two companions held that a marriage contract is valid with the wording of gift, when the woman gives herself, and he calls witnesses to a dower for himself, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his community are equal in rulings, except where the evidence makes a specific exception.

The argument of the majority is that he, peace be upon him, was specially granted the meaning of gift and its wording together, because wording follows meaning, and whoever claims that the wording is shared needs evidence.

The majority read (khāliṣatan, "exclusively") in the accusative. It is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), like (kawʿdi Allah, "the promise of Allah") and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. That is: He made it exclusive for you, an exclusivity.

﴿We have made lawful for you﴾ (khāliṣatan) in the sense of khulūṣan (exclusivity). A verbal noun comes in the pattern fāʿil and in fāʿilah. al-Zamakhshari said: the fāʿil and fāʿilah forms among verbal nouns are not rare, like khārij, qāʿid, ʿāqibah and kādhibah. He concluded, but this is not as he stated. Rather, they are rare. His example of khārij refers to the line of al-Farazdaq:

"Nor a false word coming out of my mouth."

And qāʿid, according to one of the two interpretations, refers to the line:

"Are you sitting while the caravan has set off?"

And kādhibah refers to His words: ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 2]. These words may be interpreted as not being verbal nouns.

It was read "khāliṣatun" in the nominative. Whoever takes it as a verbal noun estimates: that is an exclusivity for you, and an exclusivity apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ describe the woman who gives herself to you. So the reading in the accusative is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as stated by al-Zajjaj: We have made her lawful, exclusive for you. The nominative is the predicate of an implied subject: she is exclusive for you, that is, the giving of themselves by women is restricted to you. It is not permissible for a woman to give herself to anyone other than you.

They agreed that this is not permissible for anyone other than him, peace be upon him. It appears from the speech of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that the meaning of His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ refers to the whole of this permission, because the believers restricted themselves to two, three, or four.

al-Zamakhshari said: The evidence that it was revealed following the four permissions, specifically for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as an emphasis on that, is His words: ﴿We know what We have decreed for them concerning their wives and those their right hands possess﴾, after His words: "apart from the believers". It is a parenthetical clause (jumlah iʿtiraḍiyyah). And His words: ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ are connected to ﴿exclusively for you apart from the believers﴾ concerning wives and slave-women. And whatever description He gave, He must have decreed it for them. So He decreed it, and He knew the benefit in the exclusivity of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with what He specially granted him, and so He did it.

The meaning of ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ is: so that there will be no constriction for you in your religion, in that We have singled you out with purity, and the singling out of what is more fitting and more excellent in your worldly life, in that We have made lawful for you the kinds of women you may marry, and We have added for you the woman who gives herself. Whoever makes (khāliṣatan) a description of the woman, then according to his view: this woman is exclusive to you apart from them. End.

The apparent meaning is that (li-kayla) is connected to His words: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿so that it will not be﴾ means: We have made this explanation and clarified this clarification so that there will be no discomfort for you, and so that it is not thought of you that you have sinned before your Lord. Then He comforted all the believers with His forgiveness and mercy.

al-Zamakhshari said: (Forgiving) to the one who falls into discomfort if he repents, (Merciful) by granting ease to His servants. End. In this there is a subtle Muʿtazili insinuation.

﴿We know what We have decreed for them﴾, etc. Its meaning is: what We have mentioned is your obligation and your ruling with your wives. As for the ruling for your community, its knowledge is with Us, and We shall make it clear to them. He mentioned this only so that none of the believers would impose upon himself what was permitted for the Prophet ﷺ, for he has specific privileges in marriage and in taking slave-women which are not for anyone else.

Mujahid said: ﴿what We have decreed for them﴾ is that they must not exceed four. Qatadah said: it is the guardian (waliyy), the witnesses and the dower. It was said: what We have decreed of the dower, the maintenance and the clothing.

﴿and those their right hands possess﴾. It was said: ownership is not established except when she is of those who may lawfully be taken captive. It was said: what We permitted for them of ownership by right hand alongside the four free wives, without a limited number. The meaning is: We know the welfare of each of you and your community, and what is most beneficial for you and for them, so We legislated for your right and their right according to what We knew.

It is narrated that when his wives became jealous and sought an increase in maintenance, he abstained from them for a month, and the choice was revealed (al-takhyir). They feared being divorced, so they said: O Messenger of Allah, set for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish. The discussion of the meaning of ﴿you may postpone﴾ has preceded in His words: ﴿and others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106] in Surat Bara'ah. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (minhunna) refers to his wives, peace be upon him. Al-irjaʾ means to shelter.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: [it means] in divorcing whomever you wish of those who are in your protection, and keeping whomever you wish. Another group said: [it means] in marrying whomever you wish of those who give themselves, and delaying whomever you wish. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: and you may make whomever you wish wait in terms of the division of nights, and you may keep away from you whomever you wish, and you may reduce for whomever you wish and increase for whomever you wish; there is no discomfort upon you in that. So when they knew that this is the ruling of Allah and His decree, the rancour and jealousy were removed from them, they were satisfied, and their eyes were comforted. This accords with what was narrated about the cause of this verse, mentioned earlier.

﴿And whomever you seek from those you have set aside﴾, i.e., whomever you seek from those who were set aside and from the unmarried ones, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in taking them back and sheltering them with you. It is possible that this is an emphasis of what precedes it, meaning: whomever you seek from those you have set aside, and those you have set aside are equal; there is no blame upon you. Just as you say: whoever meets you from among those who did not meet you, all of them are grateful to you, meaning whoever met you and whoever did not meet you. In this interpretation there is an omitted conjunct, and a strangeness in indicating this meaning by this construction. The preferred view is the first.

al-Hasan said: the meaning is: whoever of your wives who are with you dies, or whom you release, there is no blame upon you in replacing her with those whom I have made lawful to you, so that you do not exceed the number of your wives who are with you.

al-Zamakhshari said: meaning you may leave aside the beds of whomever you wish of them and lie with whomever you wish; or you may divorce whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish; or you may not divide [your nights] among whichever of them you wish and divide among whomever you wish; or you may leave whomever you wish of your community and marry whomever you wish. It is narrated from al-Hasan: when the Prophet ﷺ proposed to a woman, no one could propose to her until he left her. This is a comprehensive division for the purpose intended, because he either divorces or keeps. If he keeps, he lies with her, or leaves her and divides, or does not divide. If he divorces and sets aside, then either he leaves the one set aside without following her, or he follows her.

It is narrated that he deferred from among them: Sawdah, Juwayriyah, Safiyyah, Maymunah and Umm Habibah. He would divide for them what he wished as he wished. Those he sheltered were: Aʾishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab. He deferred five and sheltered four. It is narrated that he used to treat them equally, along with what was permitted for him and granted him as a choice, except Sawdah, for she gave her night to Aʾishah and said: Do not divorce me, so that I may be raised on the Day of Resurrection among your wives. End.

That delegation to your will is closer to the comfort of their eyes, the removal of their grief, and the existence of their contentment, when you know that this delegation is from Allah. So the state of each of them is like the state of the others in this matter.

The majority read ﴿that their eyes may be comforted﴾ in the active voice, from "qarrat al-ʿayn". Ibn Muhaysin read "yuqirra", from "aqarra aʿyunahunna", in the accusative, with the subject of "tuqirra" being the second-person pronoun, i.e., you. It was also read "tuqarra" in the passive voice, with "aʿyunuhunna" in the nominative.

The majority read ﴿all of them﴾ in the nominative, as an emphasis of the subject of (yarḍayna, "they are pleased"). Abu Iyas Hawbah ibn ʿAʾidh read it in the accusative, as an emphasis of the object pronoun in ﴿you gave them﴾.

﴿And Allah knows what is in your hearts﴾ is general. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the reference here is to what is in the heart of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of love for one person over another, and the believers are included in the meaning. al-Zamakhshari and ʿUbaydah said: whoever of them is not content with what Allah wills in this matter, and delegates to the will of His Messenger, and whose hearts are inclined to agreement among themselves, sincerity among one another, and harmony in seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what brings him contentment. End. (And Allah is ever Knowing) of what the hearts harbour, (Forbearing) He pardons what overcomes the heart of the questioned, since it is something one generally does not control. The narrations agree that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to be just among them in division until he died, and he did not make use of anything of what was permitted to him, restraining himself and taking the higher path, except what happened to Sawdah, which we have mentioned.

This is Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 33, verses 49-52 (part 3 of 3).

﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾. The apparent meaning is that this ruling is muhkam (not abrogated). This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group of scholars, including al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and al-Tabari chose it. The word omitted after "مِن بَعْدُ" (min ba'd, "after this") is disputed. Ubayy, Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak said it means "after the women of whom We have made lawful for you in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾." On this meaning, women are not lawful for you after the women specified, who are lawful for you from the four categories: not a Bedouin woman, not an Arab woman, not a woman of the People of the Book, and not a slave woman by marriage. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: "after this," because nine wives were the quota (nisab) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the wives, just as four was the quota of his community from among them. They said: when they were given the choice and chose Allah and His Messenger, Allah rewarded them by forbidding him other women and by forbidding replacing them, and by this He abrogated (naskh) what He had previously permitted him of the broad latitude regarding all women. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said, and it is related from Ikrimah: "after this" means after the general permission of women, so women other than Muslim women are not lawful for you, whether a Jewish or a Christian woman. Similarly, ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them for other wives﴾ means: exchanging them for Muslim women in place of Jewish or Christian wives.

It was also said that the phrase ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them﴾ refers to the exchange (badal, substitution) that was practiced in the Jahiliyyah. A man would say: "Exchange your wife with me and I will exchange mine with you," and each of them would give up his wife to the other. Ibn Zayd said this is its meaning and that it was practiced in the Jahiliyyah. Al-Tabari and others rejected this interpretation of the verse, and the Arabs never did this at all.

As for what is related in the hadith of Uyaynah ibn Hisn, that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he entered upon him without seeking permission and Aisha was with him: "Who is this Humayra?" He said: "Aisha." Uyaynah said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you wish, I will give up for you the most distinguished of the women of the Arabs in beauty and lineage." This is not an exchange, nor did he intend it; he only belittled Aisha because she was young.

The "min" in ﴿min azwaj﴾ ("from among wives") is extra (za'idah), to emphasise the negation. Its purpose is to encompass the whole category of wives with the prohibition.

It was also said that the verse is abrogated, and scholars differed about the abrogating text. It was said to be by the Sunnah. Aisha said: "He did not die until women became lawful for him." This is related from Umm Salamah, and it is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak. It was also said to be by the Qur'an, namely His saying: ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾ and the rest of the verse. Hibat Allah al-Darir said, in his work on the abrogating and the abrogated (al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh): "There is no abrogating text in the Book of Allah that precedes the abrogated text except this one." Ibn Atiyyah said: "His statement is weak in several respects." It was also said that the saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ and so on, so the order of revelation is not the same as the order of the text in the Mushaf. It is related from Ibn Abbas that both views were transmitted: that it is muhkam, and that it is mansukh.

﴿And if her beauty pleases you﴾. It was said that among them was Asma bint Umays al-Khath'amiyyah, the wife of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. The clause, said al-Zamakhshari, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the agent, which is the pronoun in (tabaddala), and not to the object which is ﴿min azwaj﴾, because that is highly indefinite. Its implied sense is: "your admiration for them being presumed." We previously mentioned in a similar construction that it is coordinated with an omitted circumstance, i.e., ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them for other wives﴾ in every circumstance, even in this circumstance which calls for exchange, namely the state of admiration for beauty. Ibn Atiyyah said: "In this wording, ﴿if her beauty pleases you﴾, there is evidence that a man may look at the woman he wishes to marry." Indeed this is found in the Sunnah, in the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah and the hadith of Muhammad ibn Maslamah. (p-245)

﴿except what your right hand possesses﴾. That is, it is lawful for you. If "ma" is a relative pronoun referring to the genus, then this is an exception from the genus, and the nominative is preferred as a badal (substitute) for "al-nisa'" (the women). The accusative is also permissible as an exception. If "ma" is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), then it is in the accusative position, because it is an exception from something other than the first category. This is what Ibn Atiyyah said, but it is not sound. For he said: "The implied meaning is: except ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin)," and "milk" in the sense of "mamluk" (owned thing), so when it means "mamluk" it becomes part of the category of women, because he did not intend the literal verbal noun; therefore the nominative is the stronger. Also, he said: "it is in the accusative position," yet it is not necessary that it be in the accusative position. And even if we suppose that it is an exception from something other than the category literally, the Hijazi dialect uses the accusative and the Tamim use the substitute, because it is an exception in which the governing agent can be applied to it; the accusative becomes obligatory only where the exception cannot be governed by the agent, as in: "Increase did not increase the wealth except loss," where increase cannot be applied to loss. Also, he said: "an exception from something other than the genus." Malik said: "in the sense of mamluk," and thereby contradicted himself.

﴿And Allah is ever over all things an observer﴾. That is, one who watches (raqib), or one who observes (muraqib). Its meaning: a guardian, a witness, and one who is aware. This is a warning against transgressing His limits and overstepping His lawful and unlawful.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 1 of 3):

(p. 239)﴿O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period for them to count. So provide for them and release them with a fair release.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their bridal payments, and those whom your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you as spoils, and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts who emigrated with you, and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, exclusively for you, apart from the believers. We have certainly known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives and what their right hands possess, so that there will be no difficulty for you. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿You may defer whom you will of them and take to you whom you will. And whomever you seek from those you have set aside, there is no blame upon you. That is more suitable that their eyes be comforted and they not grieve and that they be pleased with what you have given them, all of them. And Allah knows what is in your hearts, and Allah is ever Knowing and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses. And Allah is ever, over all things, Watchful.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the account of Zayd and Zaynab and his divorcing her, and she had been consummated with, and had observed her waiting period, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, proposed to her after the end of her waiting period, He explained the condition of the woman who is divorced before touching (al-masis), and that there is no waiting period for her.

The meaning of ﴿nakahtum﴾ is "you contracted marriage with them." The contract was called nikah (marriage) because it is a means to it, just as intoxicants were called sin (ithm) because they are a means to it. They said: The word nikah in the Book of Allah occurs only with the meaning of the contract, and this is among the etiquettes of the Qur'an, just as it alluded to sexual intercourse with expressions such as al-mumassah, al-mulamasah, al-qurban, al-taghshshi and al-ityan. It was said: the only exception is in His saying: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:230], for it means intercourse, and the discussion of it has already passed in al-Baqarah. Although the women of the People of the Book share this ruling with the believing women, singling out the believing women for mention is an admonition that the believer should not choose for his seed except a believing woman. The purpose of bringing in ﴿thumma﴾ ("then"), although the ruling is established whether she is married and divorced immediately or whoever's divorce is delayed, is [to indicate that the ruling holds in both cases]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It negates the suspicion in the one who might suppose a difference in ruling between divorcing her while she is still recently married, and divorcing her after a long time has passed since the marriage, during which the period lengthens while the husband keeps her and then divorces her. End of quote. He used ﴿'asa﴾ ("perhaps") as a relative clause for ﴿man﴾, and that is not permissible; or it is that the predominant case was considered in this, for whoever undertakes a contract with a woman does so out of desire, so it is unlikely that he would divorce her immediately, because divorce indicates a lack of desire. Therefore there must be an interval between the contract and the divorce in which it becomes evident to the husband that he has turned away from the woman and that the benefit lies in that for him. The apparent meaning is that divorce occurs only after the contract, and the divorce of one with whom no contract was made, whether specifically, or her tribe, or her town, is not valid. This is the view of the majority among the Companions and the Successors. A large group, including Malik, said: it is valid. The apparent meaning is that al-masis here is a metaphor for intercourse, and that if he was alone with her and then divorced her, he does not [owe a waiting period]. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, the ruling for a valid seclusion (khalwah sahihah) is the ruling of touching. The apparent meaning is that a woman divorced by a revocable divorce (raj'iyyah), if her husband takes her back before her waiting period ends, and then divorces her again before touching her, does not complete her waiting period from the first pronouncement, nor begin a new waiting period, because she is a woman divorced before consummation. Dawud said likewise. ʿAta' and a group said: she continues in her waiting period from her first divorce; this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: she does not build upon the waiting period of the first divorce, but begins a new waiting period from the day he divorced her the second time. This is the view of the jurists of the majority of the regions. The apparent meaning also is that if she was irrevocably divorced (ba'in) but not thrice-divorced (mabtutah), and he married her during the waiting period and then divorced her before consummation, then, as with the revocable divorce according to Dawud's view, she has no waiting period, neither the remainder of the waiting period of the first divorce nor the beginning of a waiting period for the second, and she is owed half the dower. Al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, Ibn Shihab, Malik, al-Shafi'i, ʿUthman al-Batti and Zufar said: she is owed half the dower and completes the remainder of the first waiting period. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: she is owed the full dower for the second marriage, and a new waiting period, treating her as one who was consummated with, because her waiting period is counted from [the second marriage].

The majority recited ﴿ta'taddunaha﴾ with a doubled dal: it is the form ifta'ala from ʿadd (counting), meaning "you complete their number," from your saying: "He counted the dirhams and ta'addaha," meaning he completed their number; like your saying: "kiltuhu and iktalahu" (I measured it for him and he measured it for himself), "wazintuhu and ittazantuhu" (I weighed it and he weighed it). From Ibn Kathir and others of the people of Makkah: with a light dal. Ibn Khalawayh and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi transmitted it from Ibn Kathir. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It was related from Abu Barzah, from Ibn Kathir, with a light dal, from ʿudwan (transgression), as if he said: "You have no waiting period that you impose upon them by transgression and injustice against them." The first reading is more well-known from Ibn Kathir, and the light dal is an error by Abu Barzah. End of quote. It is not an error, for Ibn Khalawayh and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi transmitted it from Ibn Kathir in the book (Kitab al-Lawami' fi Shawadhdh al-Qira'at), and al-Razi mentioned it from the people of Makkah and said: it is from i'tidad (counting) without doubt, but they disliked the doubling, so they lightened it. If it is taken from i'tida' (transgression), which is injustice, then it is doubled, because i'tida' takes ʿala as its object. End of quote. Since it takes ʿala, it is permissible not to delete ʿala, and the verb reaches the pronoun, as in his saying:

*"She yearns and reveals what is in her of longing, and conceals what, were it not for grief, would have killed me."*

That is, it would have prevailed over me. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was read ta'taduna, lightened, meaning ta'tadunafiha (you transgress in them), like His saying: "and a day We witnessed it." And by i'tida' is meant what is in His saying: ﴿and do not keep them by harm, to transgress﴾. End of quote. He means that when the preposition is deleted, the verb is connected directly to the pronoun of the waiting period, like His saying:

*"And a day We witnessed it, Sulaym and ʿAmir."*

That is, we witnessed in it. As for [reading] with the assumption of ʿala, the meaning is: you transgress against them in it. Al-Hasan recited with a sukun on the ʿayn as the others do, and a doubled dal, combining two sukuns. His saying ﴿fa-ma lakum﴾ ("then you have none") indicates that the waiting period is predominantly a right of the husband, although it is not dropped by his waiving it, because it includes a right of Allah, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the woman divorced before touching is entitled to the provision (mut'ah) absolutely, whether her dower was specified or not. It was said: this ruling is restricted to the one for whom no dower was specified. The apparent meaning is that the command in ﴿fa-matti'uhunna﴾ is for obligation. It was said: it is for recommendation. The discussion of mut'ah has already been detailed in al-Baqarah. Al-sarah al-jamil (the fair release) is a good word without harm and without withholding what is obligatory. It was said: that he does not demand from her what he gave her.

When Allah, exalted is He, explained some of the rulings concerning the marriages of the believers, He followed it with mention of some of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-ujur means the dowers, because it is a reward (ajr) for enjoyment of the intimacy and other things permissible for enjoyment. In describing them as ﴿those whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ is an indication that Allah chose for His Prophet the more excellent and more appropriate course, because giving the dower promptly is better and more excellent than delaying it, so that the husband may discharge his obligation to the religion and clear his responsibility, and because delaying it implies that he enjoys her without any exchange she has received. Prompt payment was the custom of the predecessors, and nothing else is known from them. Do you not see his saying, peace be upon him, to one of the Companions when he complained of his marriage situation: "Where is your Hutamiyyah coat of mail?" Likewise, the restriction of what the right hand possesses by His saying ﴿from what Allah has returned to you as spoils﴾ is because if she is a captive, and he owns her from what Allah gave him as booty from the people of the land of war, she is more lawful and purer than what is bought from the slave-traders. Of those taken captive from the land of war, some said it is a captive who is pure (sabi tayyibah), and of those who have a covenant, some said it is a captive who is impure (sabi khabithah). The fay' of Allah is applied only to the pure, not the impure.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ restricts the word "wives" to those who were under his marriage, such as ʿA'ishah and Hafsah, and those he married with a dower. Ibn Zayd said: meaning those he married with a dower and those he married without a dower, and all women, even those within the prohibited degrees, of the dowered, the enslaved, and the woman who gives herself, are restricted to him. Then He said afterwards ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾, meaning from all these categories. Then the pronoun after that generalizes up to His saying ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾, so it is cut off from the first and returns to his nine wives only. In the first interpretation there is restriction. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to marry whichever of the women he wished, and that was difficult for his wives. When this verse was revealed, and women were forbidden to him by it, except those named, his wives were gratified by that. The right hand possessing is only rarely relevant, and the cousins and those mentioned with them are few. Those among them whom he could marry are limited in the view of his wives, especially since it was conditioned upon emigration, and the obligatory [portion] of women is also few, so for this reason he was gratified by the restriction of the matter. Then the coming of ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾ is an indication of what preceded, and then the coming of ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾ is an indication that his wives whose permission was previously stated explicitly by the lawful allowance, so the statement comes affirmed and consistent, more consistently than in the other interpretation.

﴿And the daughters of your paternal uncles﴾: Umm Hani bint Abi Talib said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he accepted my excuse. Then this verse was revealed and it made me unlawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him, and I was only among the freed captives (al-tulaqa'). The restriction by ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ is because whoever among his non-forbidden relatives emigrated with him is more excellent than those who did not emigrate. It was said: the condition of emigration in the permission is abrogated (mansukh). Al-Mawardi related two opinions on this: one, that emigration is a condition for the permissibility of wives absolutely; the other, that it is a condition for the permissibility of the relatives of those mentioned in the verse, but not for strangers (al-ajnabiyyat). The "with" (ma'iyyah) here is the sharing of emigration, not companionship in it. It is said: "So-and-so entered with me and left with me," meaning his action was like my action even if we did not coincide in time. If you say: "We returned together (ma'an)," both meanings imply sharing in the act and coincidence in time. He used the singular for "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" because it is a generic noun (ism jins), and likewise "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt." This is a linguistic point stated by Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi the judge.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿And a believing woman﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: she is Maymunah bint al-Harith. ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: she is Umm Sharik. ʿUrwah and al-Shaʿbi said: she is Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, Umm al-Masakin, a woman of the Ansar. ʿUrwah also said: she is Khawlah bint Hakim ibn al-Awqas al-Sulamiyyah. There is disagreement about this. From Ibn ʿAbbas: none of them was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by way of giving herself in marriage (hibah). It was also said: the women who gave themselves are four: Maymunah bint al-Harith and those mentioned before her.

The majority read (وامْرَأةً, wa-imra'atan) in the accusative (naṣb). ﴿if she gives herself﴾ is read with a kasrah on the hamzah (in, "if"). The meaning is: We have made her lawful to you if she gives herself, if he (the Prophet) desires. Here there are two conditions. The second is in the sense of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The condition for the permission is that she gives herself, and the condition for the giving is that he desires to take her in marriage (istinkah). It is as if He said: We have made her lawful to you if she gives herself to you, while you desire to marry her. His desire is his acceptance of the gift and what completes it. These two conditions are like the two conditions in His words: ﴿My advice will not benefit you if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to put you in error﴾ [Hud: 34].

When two conditions are combined, the second is a condition on the first. It is later in wording but earlier in occurrence, unless a context indicates the order, as in: "If I marry you or divorce you, then my slave is free." The combination of two conditions is a question on which there is disagreement and detail, and we have fully explained this in (Sharh al-Tashil) in the chapter on the jazm particles (al-jawazim).

Abu Haywah read: "wa-imra'atun mu'minatun" in the nominative (rafʿ), as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted. That is: We have made her lawful to you.

Ubayy, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, ʿIsa and Salam read "an" with a fathah on the hamzah. Its construction is: "li-an wahabat" (because she gave herself). This is a ruling concerning one specific woman, so the verb is past tense. The reading with the kasrah is for the future, concerning every woman who would give herself, not one specific woman. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "idh wahabat" (when she gave herself). "Idh" is an adverb of past time, so it refers to a specific woman.

He turned from address (khiṭāb) to the third person (ghaybah) regarding the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿if the Prophet desires﴾, then returned to address in His words: ﴿exclusively for you﴾, to indicate that this is among what was specially granted to him and given preference. Its coming in the wording "the Prophet" indicates that the exclusivity is an honour for him on account of prophethood. Its repetition is a glorification of him and an affirmation that he deserves this honour because of his prophethood.

Istinkah means seeking to marry her and desiring it.

The majority hold that marriage is not valid with the wording of hire (ijarah) nor with the wording of gift (hibah). Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi said: it is valid with the wording of hire, based on His words: ﴿those whose bridal payments (ujur) you have given﴾. The argument of those who prohibit it is that a contract of hire is time-limited, while a marriage contract is permanent, so the two are contradictory.

Abu Hanifah and his two companions held that a marriage contract is valid with the wording of gift, when the woman gives herself, and he calls witnesses to a dower for himself, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his community are equal in rulings, except where the evidence makes a specific exception.

The argument of the majority is that he, peace be upon him, was specially granted the meaning of gift and its wording together, because wording follows meaning, and whoever claims that the wording is shared needs evidence.

The majority read (khāliṣatan, "exclusively") in the accusative. It is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), like (kawʿdi Allah, "the promise of Allah") and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. That is: He made it exclusive for you, an exclusivity.

﴿We have made lawful for you﴾ (khāliṣatan) in the sense of khulūṣan (exclusivity). A verbal noun comes in the pattern fāʿil and in fāʿilah. al-Zamakhshari said: the fāʿil and fāʿilah forms among verbal nouns are not rare, like khārij, qāʿid, ʿāqibah and kādhibah. He concluded, but this is not as he stated. Rather, they are rare. His example of khārij refers to the line of al-Farazdaq:

"Nor a false word coming out of my mouth."

And qāʿid, according to one of the two interpretations, refers to the line:

"Are you sitting while the caravan has set off?"

And kādhibah refers to His words: ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 2]. These words may be interpreted as not being verbal nouns.

It was read "khāliṣatun" in the nominative. Whoever takes it as a verbal noun estimates: that is an exclusivity for you, and an exclusivity apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ describe the woman who gives herself to you. So the reading in the accusative is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as stated by al-Zajjaj: We have made her lawful, exclusive for you. The nominative is the predicate of an implied subject: she is exclusive for you, that is, the giving of themselves by women is restricted to you. It is not permissible for a woman to give herself to anyone other than you.

They agreed that this is not permissible for anyone other than him, peace be upon him. It appears from the speech of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that the meaning of His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ refers to the whole of this permission, because the believers restricted themselves to two, three, or four.

al-Zamakhshari said: The evidence that it was revealed following the four permissions, specifically for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as an emphasis on that, is His words: ﴿We know what We have decreed for them concerning their wives and those their right hands possess﴾, after His words: "apart from the believers". It is a parenthetical clause (jumlah iʿtiraḍiyyah). And His words: ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ are connected to ﴿exclusively for you apart from the believers﴾ concerning wives and slave-women. And whatever description He gave, He must have decreed it for them. So He decreed it, and He knew the benefit in the exclusivity of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with what He specially granted him, and so He did it.

The meaning of ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ is: so that there will be no constriction for you in your religion, in that We have singled you out with purity, and the singling out of what is more fitting and more excellent in your worldly life, in that We have made lawful for you the kinds of women you may marry, and We have added for you the woman who gives herself. Whoever makes (khāliṣatan) a description of the woman, then according to his view: this woman is exclusive to you apart from them. End.

The apparent meaning is that (li-kayla) is connected to His words: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿so that it will not be﴾ means: We have made this explanation and clarified this clarification so that there will be no discomfort for you, and so that it is not thought of you that you have sinned before your Lord. Then He comforted all the believers with His forgiveness and mercy.

al-Zamakhshari said: (Forgiving) to the one who falls into discomfort if he repents, (Merciful) by granting ease to His servants. End. In this there is a subtle Muʿtazili insinuation.

﴿We know what We have decreed for them﴾, etc. Its meaning is: what We have mentioned is your obligation and your ruling with your wives. As for the ruling for your community, its knowledge is with Us, and We shall make it clear to them. He mentioned this only so that none of the believers would impose upon himself what was permitted for the Prophet ﷺ, for he has specific privileges in marriage and in taking slave-women which are not for anyone else.

Mujahid said: ﴿what We have decreed for them﴾ is that they must not exceed four. Qatadah said: it is the guardian (waliyy), the witnesses and the dower. It was said: what We have decreed of the dower, the maintenance and the clothing.

﴿and those their right hands possess﴾. It was said: ownership is not established except when she is of those who may lawfully be taken captive. It was said: what We permitted for them of ownership by right hand alongside the four free wives, without a limited number. The meaning is: We know the welfare of each of you and your community, and what is most beneficial for you and for them, so We legislated for your right and their right according to what We knew.

It is narrated that when his wives became jealous and sought an increase in maintenance, he abstained from them for a month, and the choice was revealed (al-takhyir). They feared being divorced, so they said: O Messenger of Allah, set for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish. The discussion of the meaning of ﴿you may postpone﴾ has preceded in His words: ﴿and others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106] in Surat Bara'ah. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (minhunna) refers to his wives, peace be upon him. Al-irjaʾ means to shelter.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: [it means] in divorcing whomever you wish of those who are in your protection, and keeping whomever you wish. Another group said: [it means] in marrying whomever you wish of those who give themselves, and delaying whomever you wish. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: and you may make whomever you wish wait in terms of the division of nights, and you may keep away from you whomever you wish, and you may reduce for whomever you wish and increase for whomever you wish; there is no discomfort upon you in that. So when they knew that this is the ruling of Allah and His decree, the rancour and jealousy were removed from them, they were satisfied, and their eyes were comforted. This accords with what was narrated about the cause of this verse, mentioned earlier.

﴿And whomever you seek from those you have set aside﴾, i.e., whomever you seek from those who were set aside and from the unmarried ones, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in taking them back and sheltering them with you. It is possible that this is an emphasis of what precedes it, meaning: whomever you seek from those you have set aside, and those you have set aside are equal; there is no blame upon you. Just as you say: whoever meets you from among those who did not meet you, all of them are grateful to you, meaning whoever met you and whoever did not meet you. In this interpretation there is an omitted conjunct, and a strangeness in indicating this meaning by this construction. The preferred view is the first.

al-Hasan said: the meaning is: whoever of your wives who are with you dies, or whom you release, there is no blame upon you in replacing her with those whom I have made lawful to you, so that you do not exceed the number of your wives who are with you.

al-Zamakhshari said: meaning you may leave aside the beds of whomever you wish of them and lie with whomever you wish; or you may divorce whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish; or you may not divide [your nights] among whichever of them you wish and divide among whomever you wish; or you may leave whomever you wish of your community and marry whomever you wish. It is narrated from al-Hasan: when the Prophet ﷺ proposed to a woman, no one could propose to her until he left her. This is a comprehensive division for the purpose intended, because he either divorces or keeps. If he keeps, he lies with her, or leaves her and divides, or does not divide. If he divorces and sets aside, then either he leaves the one set aside without following her, or he follows her.

It is narrated that he deferred from among them: Sawdah, Juwayriyah, Safiyyah, Maymunah and Umm Habibah. He would divide for them what he wished as he wished. Those he sheltered were: Aʾishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab. He deferred five and sheltered four. It is narrated that he used to treat them equally, along with what was permitted for him and granted him as a choice, except Sawdah, for she gave her night to Aʾishah and said: Do not divorce me, so that I may be raised on the Day of Resurrection among your wives. End.

That delegation to your will is closer to the comfort of their eyes, the removal of their grief, and the existence of their contentment, when you know that this delegation is from Allah. So the state of each of them is like the state of the others in this matter.

The majority read ﴿that their eyes may be comforted﴾ in the active voice, from "qarrat al-ʿayn". Ibn Muhaysin read "yuqirra", from "aqarra aʿyunahunna", in the accusative, with the subject of "tuqirra" being the second-person pronoun, i.e., you. It was also read "tuqarra" in the passive voice, with "aʿyunuhunna" in the nominative.

The majority read ﴿all of them﴾ in the nominative, as an emphasis of the subject of (yarḍayna, "they are pleased"). Abu Iyas Hawbah ibn ʿAʾidh read it in the accusative, as an emphasis of the object pronoun in ﴿you gave them﴾.

﴿And Allah knows what is in your hearts﴾ is general. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the reference here is to what is in the heart of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of love for one person over another, and the believers are included in the meaning. al-Zamakhshari and ʿUbaydah said: whoever of them is not content with what Allah wills in this matter, and delegates to the will of His Messenger, and whose hearts are inclined to agreement among themselves, sincerity among one another, and harmony in seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what brings him contentment. End. (And Allah is ever Knowing) of what the hearts harbour, (Forbearing) He pardons what overcomes the heart of the questioned, since it is something one generally does not control. The narrations agree that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to be just among them in division until he died, and he did not make use of anything of what was permitted to him, restraining himself and taking the higher path, except what happened to Sawdah, which we have mentioned.

This is Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 33, verses 49-52 (part 3 of 3).

﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾. The apparent meaning is that this ruling is muhkam (not abrogated). This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group of scholars, including al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and al-Tabari chose it. The word omitted after "مِن بَعْدُ" (min ba'd, "after this") is disputed. Ubayy, Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak said it means "after the women of whom We have made lawful for you in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾." On this meaning, women are not lawful for you after the women specified, who are lawful for you from the four categories: not a Bedouin woman, not an Arab woman, not a woman of the People of the Book, and not a slave woman by marriage. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: "after this," because nine wives were the quota (nisab) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the wives, just as four was the quota of his community from among them. They said: when they were given the choice and chose Allah and His Messenger, Allah rewarded them by forbidding him other women and by forbidding replacing them, and by this He abrogated (naskh) what He had previously permitted him of the broad latitude regarding all women. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said, and it is related from Ikrimah: "after this" means after the general permission of women, so women other than Muslim women are not lawful for you, whether a Jewish or a Christian woman. Similarly, ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them for other wives﴾ means: exchanging them for Muslim women in place of Jewish or Christian wives.

It was also said that the phrase ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them﴾ refers to the exchange (badal, substitution) that was practiced in the Jahiliyyah. A man would say: "Exchange your wife with me and I will exchange mine with you," and each of them would give up his wife to the other. Ibn Zayd said this is its meaning and that it was practiced in the Jahiliyyah. Al-Tabari and others rejected this interpretation of the verse, and the Arabs never did this at all.

As for what is related in the hadith of Uyaynah ibn Hisn, that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he entered upon him without seeking permission and Aisha was with him: "Who is this Humayra?" He said: "Aisha." Uyaynah said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you wish, I will give up for you the most distinguished of the women of the Arabs in beauty and lineage." This is not an exchange, nor did he intend it; he only belittled Aisha because she was young.

The "min" in ﴿min azwaj﴾ ("from among wives") is extra (za'idah), to emphasise the negation. Its purpose is to encompass the whole category of wives with the prohibition.

It was also said that the verse is abrogated, and scholars differed about the abrogating text. It was said to be by the Sunnah. Aisha said: "He did not die until women became lawful for him." This is related from Umm Salamah, and it is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak. It was also said to be by the Qur'an, namely His saying: ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾ and the rest of the verse. Hibat Allah al-Darir said, in his work on the abrogating and the abrogated (al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh): "There is no abrogating text in the Book of Allah that precedes the abrogated text except this one." Ibn Atiyyah said: "His statement is weak in several respects." It was also said that the saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ and so on, so the order of revelation is not the same as the order of the text in the Mushaf. It is related from Ibn Abbas that both views were transmitted: that it is muhkam, and that it is mansukh.

﴿And if her beauty pleases you﴾. It was said that among them was Asma bint Umays al-Khath'amiyyah, the wife of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. The clause, said al-Zamakhshari, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the agent, which is the pronoun in (tabaddala), and not to the object which is ﴿min azwaj﴾, because that is highly indefinite. Its implied sense is: "your admiration for them being presumed." We previously mentioned in a similar construction that it is coordinated with an omitted circumstance, i.e., ﴿nor is it [lawful] to exchange them for other wives﴾ in every circumstance, even in this circumstance which calls for exchange, namely the state of admiration for beauty. Ibn Atiyyah said: "In this wording, ﴿if her beauty pleases you﴾, there is evidence that a man may look at the woman he wishes to marry." Indeed this is found in the Sunnah, in the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah and the hadith of Muhammad ibn Maslamah. (p-245)

﴿except what your right hand possesses﴾. That is, it is lawful for you. If "ma" is a relative pronoun referring to the genus, then this is an exception from the genus, and the nominative is preferred as a badal (substitute) for "al-nisa'" (the women). The accusative is also permissible as an exception. If "ma" is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), then it is in the accusative position, because it is an exception from something other than the first category. This is what Ibn Atiyyah said, but it is not sound. For he said: "The implied meaning is: except ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin)," and "milk" in the sense of "mamluk" (owned thing), so when it means "mamluk" it becomes part of the category of women, because he did not intend the literal verbal noun; therefore the nominative is the stronger. Also, he said: "it is in the accusative position," yet it is not necessary that it be in the accusative position. And even if we suppose that it is an exception from something other than the category literally, the Hijazi dialect uses the accusative and the Tamim use the substitute, because it is an exception in which the governing agent can be applied to it; the accusative becomes obligatory only where the exception cannot be governed by the agent, as in: "Increase did not increase the wealth except loss," where increase cannot be applied to loss. Also, he said: "an exception from something other than the genus." Malik said: "in the sense of mamluk," and thereby contradicted himself.

﴿And Allah is ever over all things an observer﴾. That is, one who watches (raqib), or one who observes (muraqib). Its meaning: a guardian, a witness, and one who is aware. This is a warning against transgressing His limits and overstepping His lawful and unlawful.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 1 of 3):

(p. 239)﴿O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period for them to count. So provide for them and release them with a fair release.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their bridal payments, and those whom your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you as spoils, and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts who emigrated with you, and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, exclusively for you, apart from the believers. We have certainly known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives and what their right hands possess, so that there will be no difficulty for you. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿You may defer whom you will of them and take to you whom you will. And whomever you seek from those you have set aside, there is no blame upon you. That is more suitable that their eyes be comforted and they not grieve and that they be pleased with what you have given them, all of them. And Allah knows what is in your hearts, and Allah is ever Knowing and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses. And Allah is ever, over all things, Watchful.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the account of Zayd and Zaynab and his divorcing her, and she had been consummated with, and had observed her waiting period, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, proposed to her after the end of her waiting period, He explained the condition of the woman who is divorced before touching (al-masis), and that there is no waiting period for her.

The meaning of ﴿nakahtum﴾ is "you contracted marriage with them." The contract was called nikah (marriage) because it is a means to it, just as intoxicants were called sin (ithm) because they are a means to it. They said: The word nikah in the Book of Allah occurs only with the meaning of the contract, and this is among the etiquettes of the Qur'an, just as it alluded to sexual intercourse with expressions such as al-mumassah, al-mulamasah, al-qurban, al-taghshshi and al-ityan. It was said: the only exception is in His saying: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:230], for it means intercourse, and the discussion of it has already passed in al-Baqarah. Although the women of the People of the Book share this ruling with the believing women, singling out the believing women for mention is an admonition that the believer should not choose for his seed except a believing woman. The purpose of bringing in ﴿thumma﴾ ("then"), although the ruling is established whether she is married and divorced immediately or whoever's divorce is delayed, is [to indicate that the ruling holds in both cases]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It negates the suspicion in the one who might suppose a difference in ruling between divorcing her while she is still recently married, and divorcing her after a long time has passed since the marriage, during which the period lengthens while the husband keeps her and then divorces her. End of quote. He used ﴿'asa﴾ ("perhaps") as a relative clause for ﴿man﴾, and that is not permissible; or it is that the predominant case was considered in this, for whoever undertakes a contract with a woman does so out of desire, so it is unlikely that he would divorce her immediately, because divorce indicates a lack of desire. Therefore there must be an interval between the contract and the divorce in which it becomes evident to the husband that he has turned away from the woman and that the benefit lies in that for him. The apparent meaning is that divorce occurs only after the contract, and the divorce of one with whom no contract was made, whether specifically, or her tribe, or her town, is not valid. This is the view of the majority among the Companions and the Successors. A large group, including Malik, said: it is valid. The apparent meaning is that al-masis here is a metaphor for intercourse, and that if he was alone with her and then divorced her, he does not [owe a waiting period]. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, the ruling for a valid seclusion (khalwah sahihah) is the ruling of touching. The apparent meaning is that a woman divorced by a revocable divorce (raj'iyyah), if her husband takes her back before her waiting period ends, and then divorces her again before touching her, does not complete her waiting period from the first pronouncement, nor begin a new waiting period, because she is a woman divorced before consummation. Dawud said likewise. ʿAta' and a group said: she continues in her waiting period from her first divorce; this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: she does not build upon the waiting period of the first divorce, but begins a new waiting period from the day he divorced her the second time. This is the view of the jurists of the majority of the regions. The apparent meaning also is that if she was irrevocably divorced (ba'in) but not thrice-divorced (mabtutah), and he married her during the waiting period and then divorced her before consummation, then, as with the revocable divorce according to Dawud's view, she has no waiting period, neither the remainder of the waiting period of the first divorce nor the beginning of a waiting period for the second, and she is owed half the dower. Al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, Ibn Shihab, Malik, al-Shafi'i, ʿUthman al-Batti and Zufar said: she is owed half the dower and completes the remainder of the first waiting period. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: she is owed the full dower for the second marriage, and a new waiting period, treating her as one who was consummated with, because her waiting period is counted from [the second marriage].

The majority recited ﴿ta'taddunaha﴾ with a doubled dal: it is the form ifta'ala from ʿadd (counting), meaning "you complete their number," from your saying: "He counted the dirhams and ta'addaha," meaning he completed their number; like your saying: "kiltuhu and iktalahu" (I measured it for him and he measured it for himself), "wazintuhu and ittazantuhu" (I weighed it and he weighed it). From Ibn Kathir and others of the people of Makkah: with a light dal. Ibn Khalawayh and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi transmitted it from Ibn Kathir. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It was related from Abu Barzah, from Ibn Kathir, with a light dal, from ʿudwan (transgression), as if he said: "You have no waiting period that you impose upon them by transgression and injustice against them." The first reading is more well-known from Ibn Kathir, and the light dal is an error by Abu Barzah. End of quote. It is not an error, for Ibn Khalawayh and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi transmitted it from Ibn Kathir in the book (Kitab al-Lawami' fi Shawadhdh al-Qira'at), and al-Razi mentioned it from the people of Makkah and said: it is from i'tidad (counting) without doubt, but they disliked the doubling, so they lightened it. If it is taken from i'tida' (transgression), which is injustice, then it is doubled, because i'tida' takes ʿala as its object. End of quote. Since it takes ʿala, it is permissible not to delete ʿala, and the verb reaches the pronoun, as in his saying:

*"She yearns and reveals what is in her of longing, and conceals what, were it not for grief, would have killed me."*

That is, it would have prevailed over me. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was read ta'taduna, lightened, meaning ta'tadunafiha (you transgress in them), like His saying: "and a day We witnessed it." And by i'tida' is meant what is in His saying: ﴿and do not keep them by harm, to transgress﴾. End of quote. He means that when the preposition is deleted, the verb is connected directly to the pronoun of the waiting period, like His saying:

*"And a day We witnessed it, Sulaym and ʿAmir."*

That is, we witnessed in it. As for [reading] with the assumption of ʿala, the meaning is: you transgress against them in it. Al-Hasan recited with a sukun on the ʿayn as the others do, and a doubled dal, combining two sukuns. His saying ﴿fa-ma lakum﴾ ("then you have none") indicates that the waiting period is predominantly a right of the husband, although it is not dropped by his waiving it, because it includes a right of Allah, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the woman divorced before touching is entitled to the provision (mut'ah) absolutely, whether her dower was specified or not. It was said: this ruling is restricted to the one for whom no dower was specified. The apparent meaning is that the command in ﴿fa-matti'uhunna﴾ is for obligation. It was said: it is for recommendation. The discussion of mut'ah has already been detailed in al-Baqarah. Al-sarah al-jamil (the fair release) is a good word without harm and without withholding what is obligatory. It was said: that he does not demand from her what he gave her.

When Allah, exalted is He, explained some of the rulings concerning the marriages of the believers, He followed it with mention of some of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-ujur means the dowers, because it is a reward (ajr) for enjoyment of the intimacy and other things permissible for enjoyment. In describing them as ﴿those whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ is an indication that Allah chose for His Prophet the more excellent and more appropriate course, because giving the dower promptly is better and more excellent than delaying it, so that the husband may discharge his obligation to the religion and clear his responsibility, and because delaying it implies that he enjoys her without any exchange she has received. Prompt payment was the custom of the predecessors, and nothing else is known from them. Do you not see his saying, peace be upon him, to one of the Companions when he complained of his marriage situation: "Where is your Hutamiyyah coat of mail?" Likewise, the restriction of what the right hand possesses by His saying ﴿from what Allah has returned to you as spoils﴾ is because if she is a captive, and he owns her from what Allah gave him as booty from the people of the land of war, she is more lawful and purer than what is bought from the slave-traders. Of those taken captive from the land of war, some said it is a captive who is pure (sabi tayyibah), and of those who have a covenant, some said it is a captive who is impure (sabi khabithah). The fay' of Allah is applied only to the pure, not the impure.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ restricts the word "wives" to those who were under his marriage, such as ʿA'ishah and Hafsah, and those he married with a dower. Ibn Zayd said: meaning those he married with a dower and those he married without a dower, and all women, even those within the prohibited degrees, of the dowered, the enslaved, and the woman who gives herself, are restricted to him. Then He said afterwards ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾, meaning from all these categories. Then the pronoun after that generalizes up to His saying ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾, so it is cut off from the first and returns to his nine wives only. In the first interpretation there is restriction. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to marry whichever of the women he wished, and that was difficult for his wives. When this verse was revealed, and women were forbidden to him by it, except those named, his wives were gratified by that. The right hand possessing is only rarely relevant, and the cousins and those mentioned with them are few. Those among them whom he could marry are limited in the view of his wives, especially since it was conditioned upon emigration, and the obligatory [portion] of women is also few, so for this reason he was gratified by the restriction of the matter. Then the coming of ﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾ is an indication of what preceded, and then the coming of ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾ is an indication that his wives whose permission was previously stated explicitly by the lawful allowance, so the statement comes affirmed and consistent, more consistently than in the other interpretation.

﴿And the daughters of your paternal uncles﴾: Umm Hani bint Abi Talib said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he accepted my excuse. Then this verse was revealed and it made me unlawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him, and I was only among the freed captives (al-tulaqa'). The restriction by ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ is because whoever among his non-forbidden relatives emigrated with him is more excellent than those who did not emigrate. It was said: the condition of emigration in the permission is abrogated (mansukh). Al-Mawardi related two opinions on this: one, that emigration is a condition for the permissibility of wives absolutely; the other, that it is a condition for the permissibility of the relatives of those mentioned in the verse, but not for strangers (al-ajnabiyyat). The "with" (ma'iyyah) here is the sharing of emigration, not companionship in it. It is said: "So-and-so entered with me and left with me," meaning his action was like my action even if we did not coincide in time. If you say: "We returned together (ma'an)," both meanings imply sharing in the act and coincidence in time. He used the singular for "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" because it is a generic noun (ism jins), and likewise "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt." This is a linguistic point stated by Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi the judge.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿And a believing woman﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: she is Maymunah bint al-Harith. ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: she is Umm Sharik. ʿUrwah and al-Shaʿbi said: she is Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, Umm al-Masakin, a woman of the Ansar. ʿUrwah also said: she is Khawlah bint Hakim ibn al-Awqas al-Sulamiyyah. There is disagreement about this. From Ibn ʿAbbas: none of them was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by way of giving herself in marriage (hibah). It was also said: the women who gave themselves are four: Maymunah bint al-Harith and those mentioned before her.

The majority read (وامْرَأةً, wa-imra'atan) in the accusative (naṣb). ﴿if she gives herself﴾ is read with a kasrah on the hamzah (in, "if"). The meaning is: We have made her lawful to you if she gives herself, if he (the Prophet) desires. Here there are two conditions. The second is in the sense of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The condition for the permission is that she gives herself, and the condition for the giving is that he desires to take her in marriage (istinkah). It is as if He said: We have made her lawful to you if she gives herself to you, while you desire to marry her. His desire is his acceptance of the gift and what completes it. These two conditions are like the two conditions in His words: ﴿My advice will not benefit you if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to put you in error﴾ [Hud: 34].

When two conditions are combined, the second is a condition on the first. It is later in wording but earlier in occurrence, unless a context indicates the order, as in: "If I marry you or divorce you, then my slave is free." The combination of two conditions is a question on which there is disagreement and detail, and we have fully explained this in (Sharh al-Tashil) in the chapter on the jazm particles (al-jawazim).

Abu Haywah read: "wa-imra'atun mu'minatun" in the nominative (rafʿ), as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted. That is: We have made her lawful to you.

Ubayy, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, ʿIsa and Salam read "an" with a fathah on the hamzah. Its construction is: "li-an wahabat" (because she gave herself). This is a ruling concerning one specific woman, so the verb is past tense. The reading with the kasrah is for the future, concerning every woman who would give herself, not one specific woman. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "idh wahabat" (when she gave herself). "Idh" is an adverb of past time, so it refers to a specific woman.

He turned from address (khiṭāb) to the third person (ghaybah) regarding the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿if the Prophet desires﴾, then returned to address in His words: ﴿exclusively for you﴾, to indicate that this is among what was specially granted to him and given preference. Its coming in the wording "the Prophet" indicates that the exclusivity is an honour for him on account of prophethood. Its repetition is a glorification of him and an affirmation that he deserves this honour because of his prophethood.

Istinkah means seeking to marry her and desiring it.

The majority hold that marriage is not valid with the wording of hire (ijarah) nor with the wording of gift (hibah). Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi said: it is valid with the wording of hire, based on His words: ﴿those whose bridal payments (ujur) you have given﴾. The argument of those who prohibit it is that a contract of hire is time-limited, while a marriage contract is permanent, so the two are contradictory.

Abu Hanifah and his two companions held that a marriage contract is valid with the wording of gift, when the woman gives herself, and he calls witnesses to a dower for himself, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his community are equal in rulings, except where the evidence makes a specific exception.

The argument of the majority is that he, peace be upon him, was specially granted the meaning of gift and its wording together, because wording follows meaning, and whoever claims that the wording is shared needs evidence.

The majority read (khāliṣatan, "exclusively") in the accusative. It is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), like (kawʿdi Allah, "the promise of Allah") and ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. That is: He made it exclusive for you, an exclusivity.

﴿We have made lawful for you﴾ (khāliṣatan) in the sense of khulūṣan (exclusivity). A verbal noun comes in the pattern fāʿil and in fāʿilah. al-Zamakhshari said: the fāʿil and fāʿilah forms among verbal nouns are not rare, like khārij, qāʿid, ʿāqibah and kādhibah. He concluded, but this is not as he stated. Rather, they are rare. His example of khārij refers to the line of al-Farazdaq:

"Nor a false word coming out of my mouth."

And qāʿid, according to one of the two interpretations, refers to the line:

"Are you sitting while the caravan has set off?"

And kādhibah refers to His words: ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 2]. These words may be interpreted as not being verbal nouns.

It was read "khāliṣatun" in the nominative. Whoever takes it as a verbal noun estimates: that is an exclusivity for you, and an exclusivity apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ describe the woman who gives herself to you. So the reading in the accusative is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as stated by al-Zajjaj: We have made her lawful, exclusive for you. The nominative is the predicate of an implied subject: she is exclusive for you, that is, the giving of themselves by women is restricted to you. It is not permissible for a woman to give herself to anyone other than you.

They agreed that this is not permissible for anyone other than him, peace be upon him. It appears from the speech of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that the meaning of His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ refers to the whole of this permission, because the believers restricted themselves to two, three, or four.

al-Zamakhshari said: The evidence that it was revealed following the four permissions, specifically for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as an emphasis on that, is His words: ﴿We know what We have decreed for them concerning their wives and those their right hands possess﴾, after His words: "apart from the believers". It is a parenthetical clause (jumlah iʿtiraḍiyyah). And His words: ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ are connected to ﴿exclusively for you apart from the believers﴾ concerning wives and slave-women. And whatever description He gave, He must have decreed it for them. So He decreed it, and He knew the benefit in the exclusivity of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with what He specially granted him, and so He did it.

The meaning of ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾ is: so that there will be no constriction for you in your religion, in that We have singled you out with purity, and the singling out of what is more fitting and more excellent in your worldly life, in that We have made lawful for you the kinds of women you may marry, and We have added for you the woman who gives herself. Whoever makes (khāliṣatan) a description of the woman, then according to his view: this woman is exclusive to you apart from them. End.

The apparent meaning is that (li-kayla) is connected to His words: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿so that it will not be﴾ means: We have made this explanation and clarified this clarification so that there will be no discomfort for you, and so that it is not thought of you that you have sinned before your Lord. Then He comforted all the believers with His forgiveness and mercy.

al-Zamakhshari said: (Forgiving) to the one who falls into discomfort if he repents, (Merciful) by granting ease to His servants. End. In this there is a subtle Muʿtazili insinuation.

﴿We know what We have decreed for them﴾, etc. Its meaning is: what We have mentioned is your obligation and your ruling with your wives. As for the ruling for your community, its knowledge is with Us, and We shall make it clear to them. He mentioned this only so that none of the believers would impose upon himself what was permitted for the Prophet ﷺ, for he has specific privileges in marriage and in taking slave-women which are not for anyone else.

Mujahid said: ﴿what We have decreed for them﴾ is that they must not exceed four. Qatadah said: it is the guardian (waliyy), the witnesses and the dower. It was said: what We have decreed of the dower, the maintenance and the clothing.

﴿and those their right hands possess﴾. It was said: ownership is not established except when she is of those who may lawfully be taken captive. It was said: what We permitted for them of ownership by right hand alongside the four free wives, without a limited number. The meaning is: We know the welfare of each of you and your community, and what is most beneficial for you and for them, so We legislated for your right and their right according to what We knew.

It is narrated that when his wives became jealous and sought an increase in maintenance, he abstained from them for a month, and the choice was revealed (al-takhyir). They feared being divorced, so they said: O Messenger of Allah, set for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish. The discussion of the meaning of ﴿you may postpone﴾ has preceded in His words: ﴿and others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106] in Surat Bara'ah. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (minhunna) refers to his wives, peace be upon him. Al-irjaʾ means to shelter.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: [it means] in divorcing whomever you wish of those who are in your protection, and keeping whomever you wish. Another group said: [it means] in marrying whomever you wish of those who give themselves, and delaying whomever you wish. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: and you may make whomever you wish wait in terms of the division of nights, and you may keep away from you whomever you wish, and you may reduce for whomever you wish and increase for whomever you wish; there is no discomfort upon you in that. So when they knew that this is the ruling of Allah and His decree, the rancour and jealousy were removed from them, they were satisfied, and their eyes were comforted. This accords with what was narrated about the cause of this verse, mentioned earlier.

﴿And whomever you seek from those you have set aside﴾, i.e., whomever you seek from those who were set aside and from the unmarried ones, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in taking them back and sheltering them with you. It is possible that this is an emphasis of what precedes it, meaning: whomever you seek from those you have set aside, and those you have set aside are equal; there is no blame upon you. Just as you say: whoever meets you from among those who did not meet you, all of them are grateful to you, meaning whoever met you and whoever did not meet you. In this interpretation there is an omitted conjunct, and a strangeness in indicating this meaning by this construction. The preferred view is the first.

al-Hasan said: the meaning is: whoever of your wives who are with you dies, or whom you release, there is no blame upon you in replacing her with those whom I have made lawful to you, so that you do not exceed the number of your wives who are with you.

al-Zamakhshari said: meaning you may leave aside the beds of whomever you wish of them and lie with whomever you wish; or you may divorce whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish; or you may not divide [your nights] among whichever of them you wish and divide among whomever you wish; or you may leave whomever you wish of your community and marry whomever you wish. It is narrated from al-Hasan: when the Prophet ﷺ proposed to a woman, no one could propose to her until he left her. This is a comprehensive division for the purpose intended, because he either divorces or keeps. If he keeps, he lies with her, or leaves her and divides, or does not divide. If he divorces and sets aside, then either he leaves the one set aside without following her, or he follows her.

It is narrated that he deferred from among them: Sawdah, Juwayriyah, Safiyyah, Maymunah and Umm Habibah. He would divide for them what he wished as he wished. Those he sheltered were: Aʾishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab. He deferred five and sheltered four. It is narrated that he used to treat them equally, along with what was permitted for him and granted him as a choice, except Sawdah, for she gave her night to Aʾishah and said: Do not divorce me, so that I may be raised on the Day of Resurrection among your wives. End.
