End of quote. He said "li-ma 'asa" (for what might), making "'asa" a relative clause, and this is frequently done by him, and it is not permissible. It is said regarding some jurists that the second husband, in the state of hadir al-thuluth (the final third of life, i.e., the illness of death), is treated as a punishment, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended an action that takes this into account.

﴿Whether you show something or conceal it﴾ is a warning concerning what was previously mentioned in the verse by those referred to in His saying: ﴿That is purer﴾, and those referred to in: ﴿It is not for you to offend﴾. So it was said: ﴿whether you show something﴾ with your tongues, ﴿or conceal it﴾ in your hearts, of what incurs punishment, Allah knows it, and will recompense for it. He said "something" (shay'an) so that it includes what offends him, peace be upon him, regarding their marriage and other matters, and it is applicable to every apparent and hidden thing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 33, verses 53–58 (part 2 of 2):

It is narrated that when the verse of the veil (hijab) was revealed, the fathers, the sons, and the relatives said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we also speak to them from behind a veil?" Then this was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon them﴾, meaning there is no sin upon them. Qatadah said: "This refers to leaving off the veil." Mujahid said: "This refers to removing the outer garment (jilbab) and displaying adornment." Al-Sha'bi said: "He did not mention the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle, although they are among the mahram (those who are unmarriageable to her), so that they would not describe them to the sons, and they are not among the mahram." Al-Sha'bi and Ikrimah disliked that a woman remove her headcover (khimar) in the presence of her paternal or maternal uncle. It was said: this is because the two of them are in the position of the parents, and the paternal uncle has been called "father." Some of the mahram are mentioned here, and all of them are mentioned in surah al-Nur.

Included in ﴿nor their women﴾ are the mothers, the sisters, all other kinswomen, and those who are connected to them from among the women who are close to them. Ibn Zayd and others said: it means all believing women, and the specifying of the possessive is only in the case of the right hand (aymaan). Mujahid said: it means from the people of their religion, and this is like the statement of Ibn Zayd. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur: 31] is the inclusion of male and female slaves, but not the slaves owned by others. It was said: it is restricted to female slaves. It was said: all slaves are included, whether they are owned by them or by others. Al-Nakha'i said: a female slave's master may look at what the garment covers of her body's exterior, and if the slave is a mukatab (a slave who has contracted with his master to purchase his freedom) who has the means to pay, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that the veil be set up between her and him, and Umm Salamah did this with her mukatab Nabhan.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a command to piety and a turning from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). That is, fear Allah regarding what you have been commanded concerning veiling, and Allah revealed the command regarding concealment. It seems that there is an omitted clause in the speech, and its estimate is: keep to this, and fear Allah regarding it, lest you transgress it to something else. Then He warned with His words: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾ concerning secret and open matters, the apparent and the concealed aspects of the veil, and other things. (Shahidan, "Witness") means that conditions do not vary in His knowledge.

The majority read (wa-malaa'ikatahu) with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Abbas and Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, read it in the nominative (raf'). According to the Kufan grammarians other than al-Farra', it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the position (mawdi') of the subject of inna (the grammatical structure in which the noun after inna is in the accusative). Al-Farra' stipulates that the case-ending of the subject of inna must be hidden (i.e., not visibly marked). According to the Basran grammarians, the predicate is omitted, meaning: "He sends blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and His angels send blessings." The verb (yusalluna, "they send blessings") refers back to ﴿Allah and His angels﴾. The discussion of how the two blessings are combined has already been covered in His words: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. It was also said that there is an omission in the speech, meaning: "He sends blessings, and His angels send blessings," to avoid a shared pronoun. The apparent ruling is that sending blessings and peace upon him is obligatory. It was said that it is a sunnah. If sending blessings is obligatory, it was said that it should be done each time his name is mentioned, and once in every gathering. Many virtues have come in the hadith concerning sending blessings upon him.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, some of the Companions said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, we know that; so how should we send blessings upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim, and have mercy upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You had mercy and blessed Ibrahim, among all peoples; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious." In some of the narrations there is addition and omission.

﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning those who spoke against him when he took Safiyyah bint Huyayy as a wife. End of quote. The criticism regarding the appointment of Usamah ibn Zayd: harming him (peace be upon him) and harming Allah and the Messenger is doing what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden of disbelief and sins, denying prophethood, opposing the Shari'ah (the sacred law), and the various kinds of harm they inflict upon the Messenger (ﷺ). Harm cannot be truly conceived in relation to Allah, so it was said: this is with an omitted possessive, meaning: they harm the friends of Allah. It was said: the intended meaning is harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said: regarding the harm of Allah, it is the saying of the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], ﴿Third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73], ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and: the angels are the daughters of Allah, and the idols are His partners. From Ikrimah: the act of the makers of images who fashion a creation like the creation of Allah. It was said: regarding the harm to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is their saying: "sorcerer, poet, soothsayer, madman." It was also said: it is the breaking of his canine tooth and the wounding of his face on the day of Uhud.

He applied the harm to Allah and His Messenger to the harm of the believers by His words: ﴿without what they have earned﴾, because harming the two of them can only be without right, unlike harming the believer, which may be with right. The meaning of ﴿without what they have earned﴾ is without offense and without deserving harm. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning some hypocrites who harmed Ali, may Allah honor his face, and made him hear it. It was also said: it was revealed concerning those who spread the slander against Aisha. Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and al-Kalbi said: concerning fornicators who used to pursue women while they were unwilling. It was also said: concerning Umar, who saw some suspicious behavior toward a female slave from among the female slaves of the Ansar that he disliked, so he struck her, and then the people of Umar were harmed with words, so it was revealed. Ibn Abbas said: it is narrated that Umar said one day to Ubayy: "Last night I recited ﴿And those who harm the believing men and believing women﴾, and I was alarmed by it, and indeed I strike them and scold them." So he said to him: "You are not among them; you are only a teacher and a corrector."

[p. 250] It was the custom of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) that free women and slave women would go out with their faces uncovered, wearing a shift (dir') and a headcover (khimar). Adulterers would accost them when they went out at night to attend to their needs among the palm groves and the thickets, mistaking them for slave women. Sometimes they would accost a free woman on the pretext that she was a slave, saying, "We thought she was a slave." So they were commanded to differ in their dress from the dress of slave women, by wearing outer garments (ardiyah) and wraps (malahif) and by covering their heads and faces, so that they would be modest and be respected, and so that no one would have designs on them. It is also related that in Medina there were people who would sit on the mounds (su'udat) to look at women, to confront them and to solicit them, and so this verse was revealed.

It has been said: the jalabib are the outer garments that cover from above down to the bottom. Ibn Jubayr said: they are the veils (maqani'). It has also been said: they are the wraps (malahif). It has been said: the jilbab is every garment a woman wears over her other clothes. It has also been said: it is anything with which one covers oneself, of cloth or otherwise. Abu Zayd said:

"I wrapped myself in a jilbab of the blackness of night."

It has been said: the jilbab is larger than the khimar. Ikrimah said: she casts a side of the jilbab over the rest of her body, so that it is not seen. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, when asked about this, said: that she places her outer garment above her eyebrow, then turns it around until she places it over her nose. al-Suddi said: she covers one of her eyes, her forehead, and the other side [of her face] except the eye. End of the quotation. This is also the custom in the lands of al-Andalus: nothing of the woman appears except one of her eyes. al-Kisa'i said: they should cover themselves with their wraps, drawn tight over them, meaning by "drawing tight" the sense of "bringing near" (idna'). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: this is that she winds it over the forehead and fastens it, then folds it over the nose; and even if her eyes show, it still covers the chest and most of the face.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿ونِساءِ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and the women of the believers") include both free women and slave women. The temptation regarding slave women is greater, because of how much they move about freely, unlike free women; so excluding them from the general term "women" requires a clear proof. The "min" in ﴿مِن جَلابِيبِهِنَّ﴾ ("some of their jalabib") is partitive (lil-tab'id). And ('alayhinna) "over them" covers their entire bodies, or ('alayhinna) "over them" refers to their faces, because what used to show of them in the Jahiliyyah was the face.

﴿ذَلِكَ أدْنى أنْ يُعْرَفْنَ﴾ ("That is more suitable that they be recognized") — by their chastity, by their covering, so that they are not accosted and are not addressed with what they dislike. For when a woman is in the utmost state of covering and drawing close, no one approaches her, unlike a woman who displays herself, who is open to solicitation. (وكانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا) ("and God is ever Forgiving, Merciful") is an encouragement to women to leave off covering before they were commanded to do so.

When He mentioned the state of the polytheist who harms God and His Messenger, and the openly hostile one who harms the believers, He mentioned the state of the secret one who harms God and His Messenger, while displaying the truth and concealing hypocrisy. Since those who cause harm are three, in terms of the harm they do to God, His Messenger, and the believers, the polytheists are also three: a hypocrite, one in whose heart is a disease, and a rumor-monger (murjif). The hypocrite harms in secret; the second harms the believer by pursuing his women; and the third spreads rumors about the Messenger, saying: "He has been defeated, he will be expelled from Medina, he will be seized, his expeditions have been routed." The apparent sense of the conjunction is difference by individual, so the meaning would be: "If the hypocrites do not desist from their enmity and their scheming, and the debauched from their wickedness, and the rumor-mongers from what they say of the reports of evil [lit. "news of evil"] which they spread," (p. 251) "it may also be that the difference is by attribute, so that it is one person with three attributes." Just as it came: "Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women," and He mentioned ten attributes, while the one described by them is one [group]. He specified these two attributes of the hypocrites because of how severe their harm to the believers is.

Ikrimah said: (الَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ) ("those in whose hearts is a disease") is amorousness and love of fornication, and from it is: ﴿فَيَطْمَعَ الَّذِي في قَلْبِهِ مَرَضٌ﴾ ("so that one in whose heart is a disease might be tempted") [al-Ahzab: 32]. al-Suddi said: the disease is hypocrisy, and "those in whose hearts is a disease." Ibn 'Abbas said: they are those who harmed 'Umar. al-Kalbi said: those who harm the Muslims. Ibn 'Abbas said: (المُرْجِفُونَ) ("the rumor-mongers") are those who seek out discord. Qatadah said: those who harm the hearts of the believers by suggesting killing and defeat.

﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ بِهِمْ﴾ ("We will surely set you against them") means: We will empower you over them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: We will surely guard you through them.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ فِيها﴾ ("then they will not remain your neighbors in it") means: in Medina. ﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ﴾. The conjunction was not with "fa" (then/so) because He did not intend that it be a consequence of the incitement; rather, its being the answer to the oath is more eloquent. The conjunction was with "thumma" (then), because expulsion from the homeland was greater for them than everything else they were afflicted with, so the state of expulsion is separated in time from the state of incitement. (إلّا قَلِيلًا) ("except for a little") means: a little neighborliness, or a little time, or a small number. This last is an exception from the spoken [subject], namely the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾; or qalilan is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), meaning: except as a few. The first is an exception from the verbal noun (masdar) indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the second is from the time indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. The meaning is that they will be compelled to seek expulsion from Medina for fear of being killed.

﴿مَلْعُونِينَ﴾ ("cursed") is in the accusative as a form of blame (dhamm), as al-Tabari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it could be a substitute (badal) for (قَلِيلًا) "a little." He said: it is from the exception (iqla') which we have assumed. He also allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. He said: it is as if he said: "they will be expelled from the city, cursed," and so one does not estimate ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ but estimates "they will be expelled" — this is good. End of quotation. al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and those who followed them, including Abu al-Baqa', said: it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (لا ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. al-Zamakhshari said: this is his exact wording: "cursed" is in the accusative, by way of vituperation or as a circumstantial: that is, "they will not be your neighbors except cursed." The particle of exception has entered upon the adverb of time and the circumstantial together, as was discussed in His words: ﴿إلّا أنْ يُؤْذَنَ لَكم إلى طَعامٍ غَيْرَ ناظِرِينَ إناهُ﴾ ("unless you are given permission for a meal, not waiting for its preparation") [al-Ahzab: 53]. It is not valid for it to be in the accusative from "uxidhu" (they are seized), because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it. End of quotation. The discussion with him has already been made regarding the coming of the circumstantial from what precedes it when "illa" (except) is mentioned after it, so that the exception applies to both of them; and that the majority of the Basrans prohibited this. As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's permission that it be a substitute, a substitute with a derived noun is rare. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it," this is not agreed upon, because what follows the word of condition is two things: the verb of the condition and the answer. As for the verb of the condition, al-Kisa'i permitted placing its complement before the particle, permitting: "Zayd, that he strike — strike him." As for the answer, he also permitted placing its complement before it, such as: "If Zayd honors 'Amr, he will be struck." It has been reported from some grammarians that he said the meaning is: "wherever they are found, they are seized, cursed." The correct view is that "cursed" is an attribute of "a little": that is, "except a few who are cursed," and "a little" is an exception from the waw in ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the conditional clause is also an attribute, meaning: "subdued, overpowered." The meaning of (ثُقِفُوا) is: they are confined and gained control over. The meaning of ﴿أُخِذُوا﴾ is: they are taken captive, and al-akhidh is the captive. The majority read (قُتِّلُوا) with the taa' doubled. A group read it with the taa' lightened, in which case ﴿تَقْتِيلًا﴾ is a verbal noun not according to the regular pattern of verbal nouns.

The apparent meaning is that the hypocrites ceased from what they used to harm the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with, and all of them concealed themselves and held back, out of fear that what the oath was sworn about would befall them: the incitement, the expulsion, the seizing, and the killing. It has been said: they did not fully comply with desisting, nor was the threat carried out against them in full. Do you not see their expulsion from the mosque, his prohibition of praying over them, and what was revealed about them in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah)? And far from the truth is the one who went to the view that these categories did not desist and God did not carry out the threat against them, so in this is evidence against the doctrine of the execution of threats in the Hereafter; and this threat would then be conditional and subject to God's will.

(سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ) ("the way of God") is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: God has established, regarding those who oppose the prophets in hypocrisy, that they be killed wherever they are found. It is related from Muqatil: as those of the people of Badr were killed and taken captive. Thus "those who passed away before" includes the followers of the prophets who were hypocrites, and those who were killed on the day of Badr.

﴿يَسْألُكَ النّاسُ﴾ ("people ask you") means: the polytheists, about the time of the coming of the Hour, seeking it hastily as a form of mockery; and the Jews as a form of testing, since its time was concealed in the Torah. So the verse was revealed to refer knowledge to God, since He has not informed any angel or prophet of it. When He mentioned their state in this world, that they are cursed, humiliated, and killed, He explained their state in the Hereafter. (وما يُدْرِيكَ) ("and what will make you know") — "what" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence, meaning: "and what thing makes you know of it?" Its meaning is negation, that is: no one knows of it.

﴿لَعَلَّ السّاعَةَ تَكُونُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("perhaps the Hour is near") — He explained the nearness of the Hour; in this there is consolation for the one being tested and a warning for the one who is hasty. (قَرِيبًا) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: in a near time, since its use as an adverb is very common; it is also used not as an adverb, as you say: "Indeed, near you is Zayd," so it is permissible that the estimate be: "a near thing." Or "the Hour" means "the time," so (قَرِيبًا) is masculine according to the meaning. Or the estimate is: "perhaps the coming of the Hour," so "the Hour" is considered in (تَكُونُ), and so it is feminine; and the omitted genitive construct, which is "the coming" (qiyam), is considered in (قَرِيبًا), and so it is masculine.

﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾. (Yawma), "the Day," may be in the accusative, governed by (lā yajidūn), "they will not find," and then (yaqūlūn), "they will say," is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) informing about them. Or the speech is complete at their saying (wa lā naṣīran), "nor any helper." (Yawma) may also be governed by (yaqūlūn), "they will say," or by an elided verb, meaning: remember (udhkur), and then (yaqūlūn) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read (tuqallabu), in the passive form. Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Ruʾāsī read it with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, meaning (tataqallabu), "they turn over." Ibn ʿAṭiyya related this from Abū Ḥaywa. Ibn Khālawayh said, on the authority of Abū Ḥaywa: (nuqallibu), with a nūn, and (wujūhahum) in the accusative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also related this from Abū Ḥaywa and from Khārija. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ added that it is the reading of ʿĪsā al-Baṣrī. ʿĪsā al-Kūfī read it likewise, except that the nūn is replaced by a tāʾ. The subject of (tuqallabu) is a pronoun referring to (saʿīran), "the blaze," and to Jahannam, which is attributed to both by way of extended usage (ittisāʿan). The reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla is (tataqallabu) with two tāʾs.

The turning of faces in the Fire means their moving in different directions, or their being changed from their forms, or their being thrown into the Fire upside down. The apparent meaning is the first. The face is the most noble part of a human being, so if it is turned over in the Fire, the turning of everything else is more fitting. The face is used here to refer to the whole person. Their wish (to obey), where it is no longer of benefit, and their complaint about their great ones, is of no use.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sādatanā﴾, "our masters," as a plural on the pattern (faʿalāt). Its original form is (sudah), and this is anomalous (shādhdh) for the plural of (fayʿil). If it is taken as the plural of (sāʾid), it comes close to the regular pattern. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, al-Sulamī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and the common readers in al-Jāmiʿ in Basra read (sādātanā) with the plural suffix alif-tāʾ, which is not a regular pattern, as in (sūqāt) and (mawālīyāt) of the Banū Hāshim.

Their masters (sādatuhum) are the leaders of disbelief who instilled disbelief in them and made it appear attractive to them. Qatāda said: sādatunā means our leaders. Ṭāwūs said: our nobles. Abū Usāma said: our rulers. And the poet said:

*Tasalsala qawmun sādatun thumma zādatun*
*yubdūna ahla al-jamʿi yawma al-muḥaṣṣabi*

(A people of masters came in succession, then more of them,
showing the people of the gathering on the Day of al-Muḥaṣṣab.)

It is said: (ḍalla al-sabīl) and (ḍalla ʿan al-sabīl), "he strayed from the path." When the hamza of transitivity (hamzat al-naql) is added, the verb becomes transitive to two objects. The discussion of the alif in (al-rasūlā) and (al-sabīlā) in the verse (wa taẓunnūna billāhi al-ẓunūnā), "and you assumed about God assumptions" (33:10), has already preceded.

Since their wish did not benefit them to believe through obedience to God and His Messenger, and since no excuse stood for them in their complaint against those who led them astray, they called down (a curse) upon their masters.

﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾: a double portion of punishment for their own straying, and a double portion for leading astray those whom they led astray. Al-Jumhur read (kathīran), with the thāʾ (ث). Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿraj, according to one report from him, read it with the bāʾ (ب), i.e., (kabīran), "great."

﴿Like those who harmed Moses﴾. It was said: this was revealed concerning the affair of Zayd and Zaynab, and what was heard about it from some people's talk. It was also said: what is meant is the story of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk), on the basis that no prophet was harmed as you were harmed. In the hadith of the man who said about a division that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had made: "This is a division by which the face of God was not sought," and became angry and said: "May God have mercy on my brother Moses; he was harmed more than this and was patient." The harming of Moses consisted of their saying that he had a skin disease (abraṣ) and a swelling of the testicles (ādar), and that he envied his brother Hārūn and killed him. Or it is the story of the hired prostitute who was to claim that Moses had committed fornication with her. Or it is what they attributed to him of sorcery and madness. These are the opinions.

﴿From what they said﴾: that is, from the accusation (wasm) of what they said. (Mā), "what," may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya).

﴿And he was honored in the sight of God﴾. Al-Jumhur read (ʿinda Allāh) with the adverbial phrase governing (wajīhan), meaning: having standing and rank before God, the Exalted, who removes harm from him and repels accusations. ʿAbd Allāh, al-Aʿmash, and Abū Ḥaywa read (ʿabdun), from servitude (ʿubūdiyya), with the (lām) of the preposition (lillāh) in the genitive, and (ʿabdan) as the predicate of (kāna), and (wajīhan) as its attribute. Ibn Khālawayh said: I prayed behind Ibn Shanabūdh in the month of Ramadan, and I heard him recite: (wa kāna ʿabdu Allāh), in accordance with the reading of Ibn Masʿūd.

Ibn Zayd said: (wajīhan) means accepted. Al-Ḥasan said: one whose supplication is answered; he asked for nothing except that he was given it, except seeing God in this world. Quṭrub said: of high rank. It was also said: his standing was that God spoke to him and gave him the title Kalīm Allāh, "the one who spoke with God."

The word (sadīd) has already been explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: here it means correct (ṣawāb). Muqātil and Qatāda said: upright (sadīdan) concerning the affair of Zayd, Zaynab, and the Messenger. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima also said: "There is no god but God." It was said: what its outward meaning agrees with its inward meaning. It was said: it is correction, from straightening the arrow so that it hits the target. It was also said: (sadīd) includes all good things.

Righteous deeds and the forgiveness of sins are made to follow from the upright word. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this verse confirms the one before it. That one was built upon the prohibition against what harms the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this one upon the command to fear God in guarding the tongue, so that prohibition and command follow one another upon them. The prohibition is followed by what contains a warning, in the story of Moses, and the command is followed by a far-reaching promise. Thus the restraint against harm and the motive to abandon it become stronger. End. It is a fine statement.

[p. 250] It was the custom of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) that free women and slave women would go out with their faces uncovered, wearing a shift (dir') and a headcover (khimar). Adulterers would accost them when they went out at night to attend to their needs among the palm groves and the thickets, mistaking them for slave women. Sometimes they would accost a free woman on the pretext that she was a slave, saying, "We thought she was a slave." So they were commanded to differ in their dress from the dress of slave women, by wearing outer garments (ardiyah) and wraps (malahif) and by covering their heads and faces, so that they would be modest and be respected, and so that no one would have designs on them. It is also related that in Medina there were people who would sit on the mounds (su'udat) to look at women, to confront them and to solicit them, and so this verse was revealed.

It has been said: the jalabib are the outer garments that cover from above down to the bottom. Ibn Jubayr said: they are the veils (maqani'). It has also been said: they are the wraps (malahif). It has been said: the jilbab is every garment a woman wears over her other clothes. It has also been said: it is anything with which one covers oneself, of cloth or otherwise. Abu Zayd said:

"I wrapped myself in a jilbab of the blackness of night."

It has been said: the jilbab is larger than the khimar. Ikrimah said: she casts a side of the jilbab over the rest of her body, so that it is not seen. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, when asked about this, said: that she places her outer garment above her eyebrow, then turns it around until she places it over her nose. al-Suddi said: she covers one of her eyes, her forehead, and the other side [of her face] except the eye. End of the quotation. This is also the custom in the lands of al-Andalus: nothing of the woman appears except one of her eyes. al-Kisa'i said: they should cover themselves with their wraps, drawn tight over them, meaning by "drawing tight" the sense of "bringing near" (idna'). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: this is that she winds it over the forehead and fastens it, then folds it over the nose; and even if her eyes show, it still covers the chest and most of the face.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿ونِساءِ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and the women of the believers") include both free women and slave women. The temptation regarding slave women is greater, because of how much they move about freely, unlike free women; so excluding them from the general term "women" requires a clear proof. The "min" in ﴿مِن جَلابِيبِهِنَّ﴾ ("some of their jalabib") is partitive (lil-tab'id). And ('alayhinna) "over them" covers their entire bodies, or ('alayhinna) "over them" refers to their faces, because what used to show of them in the Jahiliyyah was the face.

﴿ذَلِكَ أدْنى أنْ يُعْرَفْنَ﴾ ("That is more suitable that they be recognized") — by their chastity, by their covering, so that they are not accosted and are not addressed with what they dislike. For when a woman is in the utmost state of covering and drawing close, no one approaches her, unlike a woman who displays herself, who is open to solicitation. (وكانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا) ("and God is ever Forgiving, Merciful") is an encouragement to women to leave off covering before they were commanded to do so.

When He mentioned the state of the polytheist who harms God and His Messenger, and the openly hostile one who harms the believers, He mentioned the state of the secret one who harms God and His Messenger, while displaying the truth and concealing hypocrisy. Since those who cause harm are three, in terms of the harm they do to God, His Messenger, and the believers, the polytheists are also three: a hypocrite, one in whose heart is a disease, and a rumor-monger (murjif). The hypocrite harms in secret; the second harms the believer by pursuing his women; and the third spreads rumors about the Messenger, saying: "He has been defeated, he will be expelled from Medina, he will be seized, his expeditions have been routed." The apparent sense of the conjunction is difference by individual, so the meaning would be: "If the hypocrites do not desist from their enmity and their scheming, and the debauched from their wickedness, and the rumor-mongers from what they say of the reports of evil [lit. "news of evil"] which they spread," (p. 251) "it may also be that the difference is by attribute, so that it is one person with three attributes." Just as it came: "Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women," and He mentioned ten attributes, while the one described by them is one [group]. He specified these two attributes of the hypocrites because of how severe their harm to the believers is.

Ikrimah said: (الَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ) ("those in whose hearts is a disease") is amorousness and love of fornication, and from it is: ﴿فَيَطْمَعَ الَّذِي في قَلْبِهِ مَرَضٌ﴾ ("so that one in whose heart is a disease might be tempted") [al-Ahzab: 32]. al-Suddi said: the disease is hypocrisy, and "those in whose hearts is a disease." Ibn 'Abbas said: they are those who harmed 'Umar. al-Kalbi said: those who harm the Muslims. Ibn 'Abbas said: (المُرْجِفُونَ) ("the rumor-mongers") are those who seek out discord. Qatadah said: those who harm the hearts of the believers by suggesting killing and defeat.

﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ بِهِمْ﴾ ("We will surely set you against them") means: We will empower you over them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: We will surely guard you through them.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ فِيها﴾ ("then they will not remain your neighbors in it") means: in Medina. ﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ﴾. The conjunction was not with "fa" (then/so) because He did not intend that it be a consequence of the incitement; rather, its being the answer to the oath is more eloquent. The conjunction was with "thumma" (then), because expulsion from the homeland was greater for them than everything else they were afflicted with, so the state of expulsion is separated in time from the state of incitement. (إلّا قَلِيلًا) ("except for a little") means: a little neighborliness, or a little time, or a small number. This last is an exception from the spoken [subject], namely the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾; or qalilan is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), meaning: except as a few. The first is an exception from the verbal noun (masdar) indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the second is from the time indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. The meaning is that they will be compelled to seek expulsion from Medina for fear of being killed.

﴿مَلْعُونِينَ﴾ ("cursed") is in the accusative as a form of blame (dhamm), as al-Tabari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it could be a substitute (badal) for (قَلِيلًا) "a little." He said: it is from the exception (iqla') which we have assumed. He also allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. He said: it is as if he said: "they will be expelled from the city, cursed," and so one does not estimate ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ but estimates "they will be expelled" — this is good. End of quotation. al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and those who followed them, including Abu al-Baqa', said: it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (لا ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. al-Zamakhshari said: this is his exact wording: "cursed" is in the accusative, by way of vituperation or as a circumstantial: that is, "they will not be your neighbors except cursed." The particle of exception has entered upon the adverb of time and the circumstantial together, as was discussed in His words: ﴿إلّا أنْ يُؤْذَنَ لَكم إلى طَعامٍ غَيْرَ ناظِرِينَ إناهُ﴾ ("unless you are given permission for a meal, not waiting for its preparation") [al-Ahzab: 53]. It is not valid for it to be in the accusative from "uxidhu" (they are seized), because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it. End of quotation. The discussion with him has already been made regarding the coming of the circumstantial from what precedes it when "illa" (except) is mentioned after it, so that the exception applies to both of them; and that the majority of the Basrans prohibited this. As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's permission that it be a substitute, a substitute with a derived noun is rare. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it," this is not agreed upon, because what follows the word of condition is two things: the verb of the condition and the answer. As for the verb of the condition, al-Kisa'i permitted placing its complement before the particle, permitting: "Zayd, that he strike — strike him." As for the answer, he also permitted placing its complement before it, such as: "If Zayd honors 'Amr, he will be struck." It has been reported from some grammarians that he said the meaning is: "wherever they are found, they are seized, cursed." The correct view is that "cursed" is an attribute of "a little": that is, "except a few who are cursed," and "a little" is an exception from the waw in ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the conditional clause is also an attribute, meaning: "subdued, overpowered." The meaning of (ثُقِفُوا) is: they are confined and gained control over. The meaning of ﴿أُخِذُوا﴾ is: they are taken captive, and al-akhidh is the captive. The majority read (قُتِّلُوا) with the taa' doubled. A group read it with the taa' lightened, in which case ﴿تَقْتِيلًا﴾ is a verbal noun not according to the regular pattern of verbal nouns.

The apparent meaning is that the hypocrites ceased from what they used to harm the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with, and all of them concealed themselves and held back, out of fear that what the oath was sworn about would befall them: the incitement, the expulsion, the seizing, and the killing. It has been said: they did not fully comply with desisting, nor was the threat carried out against them in full. Do you not see their expulsion from the mosque, his prohibition of praying over them, and what was revealed about them in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah)? And far from the truth is the one who went to the view that these categories did not desist and God did not carry out the threat against them, so in this is evidence against the doctrine of the execution of threats in the Hereafter; and this threat would then be conditional and subject to God's will.

(سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ) ("the way of God") is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: God has established, regarding those who oppose the prophets in hypocrisy, that they be killed wherever they are found. It is related from Muqatil: as those of the people of Badr were killed and taken captive. Thus "those who passed away before" includes the followers of the prophets who were hypocrites, and those who were killed on the day of Badr.

﴿يَسْألُكَ النّاسُ﴾ ("people ask you") means: the polytheists, about the time of the coming of the Hour, seeking it hastily as a form of mockery; and the Jews as a form of testing, since its time was concealed in the Torah. So the verse was revealed to refer knowledge to God, since He has not informed any angel or prophet of it. When He mentioned their state in this world, that they are cursed, humiliated, and killed, He explained their state in the Hereafter. (وما يُدْرِيكَ) ("and what will make you know") — "what" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence, meaning: "and what thing makes you know of it?" Its meaning is negation, that is: no one knows of it.

﴿لَعَلَّ السّاعَةَ تَكُونُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("perhaps the Hour is near") — He explained the nearness of the Hour; in this there is consolation for the one being tested and a warning for the one who is hasty. (قَرِيبًا) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: in a near time, since its use as an adverb is very common; it is also used not as an adverb, as you say: "Indeed, near you is Zayd," so it is permissible that the estimate be: "a near thing." Or "the Hour" means "the time," so (قَرِيبًا) is masculine according to the meaning. Or the estimate is: "perhaps the coming of the Hour," so "the Hour" is considered in (تَكُونُ), and so it is feminine; and the omitted genitive construct, which is "the coming" (qiyam), is considered in (قَرِيبًا), and so it is masculine.

﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾. (Yawma), "the Day," may be in the accusative, governed by (lā yajidūn), "they will not find," and then (yaqūlūn), "they will say," is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) informing about them. Or the speech is complete at their saying (wa lā naṣīran), "nor any helper." (Yawma) may also be governed by (yaqūlūn), "they will say," or by an elided verb, meaning: remember (udhkur), and then (yaqūlūn) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read (tuqallabu), in the passive form. Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Ruʾāsī read it with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, meaning (tataqallabu), "they turn over." Ibn ʿAṭiyya related this from Abū Ḥaywa. Ibn Khālawayh said, on the authority of Abū Ḥaywa: (nuqallibu), with a nūn, and (wujūhahum) in the accusative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also related this from Abū Ḥaywa and from Khārija. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ added that it is the reading of ʿĪsā al-Baṣrī. ʿĪsā al-Kūfī read it likewise, except that the nūn is replaced by a tāʾ. The subject of (tuqallabu) is a pronoun referring to (saʿīran), "the blaze," and to Jahannam, which is attributed to both by way of extended usage (ittisāʿan). The reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla is (tataqallabu) with two tāʾs.

The turning of faces in the Fire means their moving in different directions, or their being changed from their forms, or their being thrown into the Fire upside down. The apparent meaning is the first. The face is the most noble part of a human being, so if it is turned over in the Fire, the turning of everything else is more fitting. The face is used here to refer to the whole person. Their wish (to obey), where it is no longer of benefit, and their complaint about their great ones, is of no use.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sādatanā﴾, "our masters," as a plural on the pattern (faʿalāt). Its original form is (sudah), and this is anomalous (shādhdh) for the plural of (fayʿil). If it is taken as the plural of (sāʾid), it comes close to the regular pattern. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, al-Sulamī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and the common readers in al-Jāmiʿ in Basra read (sādātanā) with the plural suffix alif-tāʾ, which is not a regular pattern, as in (sūqāt) and (mawālīyāt) of the Banū Hāshim.

Their masters (sādatuhum) are the leaders of disbelief who instilled disbelief in them and made it appear attractive to them. Qatāda said: sādatunā means our leaders. Ṭāwūs said: our nobles. Abū Usāma said: our rulers. And the poet said:

*Tasalsala qawmun sādatun thumma zādatun*
*yubdūna ahla al-jamʿi yawma al-muḥaṣṣabi*

(A people of masters came in succession, then more of them,
showing the people of the gathering on the Day of al-Muḥaṣṣab.)

It is said: (ḍalla al-sabīl) and (ḍalla ʿan al-sabīl), "he strayed from the path." When the hamza of transitivity (hamzat al-naql) is added, the verb becomes transitive to two objects. The discussion of the alif in (al-rasūlā) and (al-sabīlā) in the verse (wa taẓunnūna billāhi al-ẓunūnā), "and you assumed about God assumptions" (33:10), has already preceded.

Since their wish did not benefit them to believe through obedience to God and His Messenger, and since no excuse stood for them in their complaint against those who led them astray, they called down (a curse) upon their masters.

﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾: a double portion of punishment for their own straying, and a double portion for leading astray those whom they led astray. Al-Jumhur read (kathīran), with the thāʾ (ث). Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿraj, according to one report from him, read it with the bāʾ (ب), i.e., (kabīran), "great."

﴿Like those who harmed Moses﴾. It was said: this was revealed concerning the affair of Zayd and Zaynab, and what was heard about it from some people's talk. It was also said: what is meant is the story of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk), on the basis that no prophet was harmed as you were harmed. In the hadith of the man who said about a division that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had made: "This is a division by which the face of God was not sought," and became angry and said: "May God have mercy on my brother Moses; he was harmed more than this and was patient." The harming of Moses consisted of their saying that he had a skin disease (abraṣ) and a swelling of the testicles (ādar), and that he envied his brother Hārūn and killed him. Or it is the story of the hired prostitute who was to claim that Moses had committed fornication with her. Or it is what they attributed to him of sorcery and madness. These are the opinions.

﴿From what they said﴾: that is, from the accusation (wasm) of what they said. (Mā), "what," may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya).

﴿And he was honored in the sight of God﴾. Al-Jumhur read (ʿinda Allāh) with the adverbial phrase governing (wajīhan), meaning: having standing and rank before God, the Exalted, who removes harm from him and repels accusations. ʿAbd Allāh, al-Aʿmash, and Abū Ḥaywa read (ʿabdun), from servitude (ʿubūdiyya), with the (lām) of the preposition (lillāh) in the genitive, and (ʿabdan) as the predicate of (kāna), and (wajīhan) as its attribute. Ibn Khālawayh said: I prayed behind Ibn Shanabūdh in the month of Ramadan, and I heard him recite: (wa kāna ʿabdu Allāh), in accordance with the reading of Ibn Masʿūd.

Ibn Zayd said: (wajīhan) means accepted. Al-Ḥasan said: one whose supplication is answered; he asked for nothing except that he was given it, except seeing God in this world. Quṭrub said: of high rank. It was also said: his standing was that God spoke to him and gave him the title Kalīm Allāh, "the one who spoke with God."

The word (sadīd) has already been explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: here it means correct (ṣawāb). Muqātil and Qatāda said: upright (sadīdan) concerning the affair of Zayd, Zaynab, and the Messenger. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima also said: "There is no god but God." It was said: what its outward meaning agrees with its inward meaning. It was said: it is correction, from straightening the arrow so that it hits the target. It was also said: (sadīd) includes all good things.

Righteous deeds and the forgiveness of sins are made to follow from the upright word. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this verse confirms the one before it. That one was built upon the prohibition against what harms the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this one upon the command to fear God in guarding the tongue, so that prohibition and command follow one another upon them. The prohibition is followed by what contains a warning, in the story of Moses, and the command is followed by a far-reaching promise. Thus the restraint against harm and the motive to abandon it become stronger. End. It is a fine statement.

(إلّا قَلِيلًا) ("except for a little") means: a little neighborliness, or a little time, or a small number. This last is an exception from the spoken [subject], namely the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾; or qalilan is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), meaning: except as a few. The first is an exception from the verbal noun (masdar) indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the second is from the time indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. The meaning is that they will be compelled to seek expulsion from Medina for fear of being killed.

﴿مَلْعُونِينَ﴾ ("cursed") is in the accusative as a form of blame (dhamm), as al-Tabari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it could be a substitute (badal) for (قَلِيلًا) "a little." He said: it is from the exception (iqla') which we have assumed. He also allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. He said: it is as if he said: "they will be expelled from the city, cursed," and so one does not estimate ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ but estimates "they will be expelled" — this is good. End of quotation. al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and those who followed them, including Abu al-Baqa', said: it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (لا ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. al-Zamakhshari said: this is his exact wording: "cursed" is in the accusative, by way of vituperation or as a circumstantial: that is, "they will not be your neighbors except cursed." The particle of exception has entered upon the adverb of time and the circumstantial together, as was discussed in His words: ﴿إلّا أنْ يُؤْذَنَ لَكم إلى طَعامٍ غَيْرَ ناظِرِينَ إناهُ﴾ ("unless you are given permission for a meal, not waiting for its preparation") [al-Ahzab: 53]. It is not valid for it to be in the accusative from "uxidhu" (they are seized), because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it. End of quotation. The discussion with him has already been made regarding the coming of the circumstantial from what precedes it when "illa" (except) is mentioned after it, so that the exception applies to both of them; and that the majority of the Basrans prohibited this. As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's permission that it be a substitute, a substitute with a derived noun is rare. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "because what follows the word of condition does not govern what precedes it," this is not agreed upon, because what follows the word of condition is two things: the verb of the condition and the answer. As for the verb of the condition, al-Kisa'i permitted placing its complement before the particle, permitting: "Zayd, that he strike — strike him." As for the answer, he also permitted placing its complement before it, such as: "If Zayd honors 'Amr, he will be struck." It has been reported from some grammarians that he said the meaning is: "wherever they are found, they are seized, cursed." The correct view is that "cursed" is an attribute of "a little": that is, "except a few who are cursed," and "a little" is an exception from the waw in ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the conditional clause is also an attribute, meaning: "subdued, overpowered." The meaning of (ثُقِفُوا) is: they are confined and gained control over. The meaning of ﴿أُخِذُوا﴾ is: they are taken captive, and al-akhidh is the captive. The majority read (قُتِّلُوا) with the taa' doubled. A group read it with the taa' lightened, in which case ﴿تَقْتِيلًا﴾ is a verbal noun not according to the regular pattern of verbal nouns.

The apparent meaning is that the hypocrites ceased from what they used to harm the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with, and all of them concealed themselves and held back, out of fear that what the oath was sworn about would befall them: the incitement, the expulsion, the seizing, and the killing. It has been said: they did not fully comply with desisting, nor was the threat carried out against them in full. Do you not see their expulsion from the mosque, his prohibition of praying over them, and what was revealed about them in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah)? And far from the truth is the one who went to the view that these categories did not desist and God did not carry out the threat against them, so in this is evidence against the doctrine of the execution of threats in the Hereafter; and this threat would then be conditional and subject to God's will.

(سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ) ("the way of God") is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: God has established, regarding those who oppose the prophets in hypocrisy, that they be killed wherever they are found. It is related from Muqatil: as those of the people of Badr were killed and taken captive. Thus "those who passed away before" includes the followers of the prophets who were hypocrites, and those who were killed on the day of Badr.

﴿يَسْألُكَ النّاسُ﴾ ("people ask you") means: the polytheists, about the time of the coming of the Hour, seeking it hastily as a form of mockery; and the Jews as a form of testing, since its time was concealed in the Torah. So the verse was revealed to refer knowledge to God, since He has not informed any angel or prophet of it. When He mentioned their state in this world, that they are cursed, humiliated, and killed, He explained their state in the Hereafter. (وما يُدْرِيكَ) ("and what will make you know") — "what" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence, meaning: "and what thing makes you know of it?" Its meaning is negation, that is: no one knows of it.

﴿لَعَلَّ السّاعَةَ تَكُونُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("perhaps the Hour is near") — He explained the nearness of the Hour; in this there is consolation for the one being tested and a warning for the one who is hasty. (قَرِيبًا) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: in a near time, since its use as an adverb is very common; it is also used not as an adverb, as you say: "Indeed, near you is Zayd," so it is permissible that the estimate be: "a near thing." Or "the Hour" means "the time," so (قَرِيبًا) is masculine according to the meaning. Or the estimate is: "perhaps the coming of the Hour," so "the Hour" is considered in (تَكُونُ), and so it is feminine; and the omitted genitive construct, which is "the coming" (qiyam), is considered in (قَرِيبًا), and so it is masculine.

﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾. (Yawma), "the Day," may be in the accusative, governed by (lā yajidūn), "they will not find," and then (yaqūlūn), "they will say," is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) informing about them. Or the speech is complete at their saying (wa lā naṣīran), "nor any helper." (Yawma) may also be governed by (yaqūlūn), "they will say," or by an elided verb, meaning: remember (udhkur), and then (yaqūlūn) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read (tuqallabu), in the passive form. Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Ruʾāsī read it with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, meaning (tataqallabu), "they turn over." Ibn ʿAṭiyya related this from Abū Ḥaywa. Ibn Khālawayh said, on the authority of Abū Ḥaywa: (nuqallibu), with a nūn, and (wujūhahum) in the accusative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also related this from Abū Ḥaywa and from Khārija. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ added that it is the reading of ʿĪsā al-Baṣrī. ʿĪsā al-Kūfī read it likewise, except that the nūn is replaced by a tāʾ. The subject of (tuqallabu) is a pronoun referring to (saʿīran), "the blaze," and to Jahannam, which is attributed to both by way of extended usage (ittisāʿan). The reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla is (tataqallabu) with two tāʾs.

The turning of faces in the Fire means their moving in different directions, or their being changed from their forms, or their being thrown into the Fire upside down. The apparent meaning is the first. The face is the most noble part of a human being, so if it is turned over in the Fire, the turning of everything else is more fitting. The face is used here to refer to the whole person. Their wish (to obey), where it is no longer of benefit, and their complaint about their great ones, is of no use.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sādatanā﴾, "our masters," as a plural on the pattern (faʿalāt). Its original form is (sudah), and this is anomalous (shādhdh) for the plural of (fayʿil). If it is taken as the plural of (sāʾid), it comes close to the regular pattern. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, al-Sulamī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and the common readers in al-Jāmiʿ in Basra read (sādātanā) with the plural suffix alif-tāʾ, which is not a regular pattern, as in (sūqāt) and (mawālīyāt) of the Banū Hāshim.

Their masters (sādatuhum) are the leaders of disbelief who instilled disbelief in them and made it appear attractive to them. Qatāda said: sādatunā means our leaders. Ṭāwūs said: our nobles. Abū Usāma said: our rulers. And the poet said:

*Tasalsala qawmun sādatun thumma zādatun*
*yubdūna ahla al-jamʿi yawma al-muḥaṣṣabi*

(A people of masters came in succession, then more of them,
showing the people of the gathering on the Day of al-Muḥaṣṣab.)

It is said: (ḍalla al-sabīl) and (ḍalla ʿan al-sabīl), "he strayed from the path." When the hamza of transitivity (hamzat al-naql) is added, the verb becomes transitive to two objects. The discussion of the alif in (al-rasūlā) and (al-sabīlā) in the verse (wa taẓunnūna billāhi al-ẓunūnā), "and you assumed about God assumptions" (33:10), has already preceded.

Since their wish did not benefit them to believe through obedience to God and His Messenger, and since no excuse stood for them in their complaint against those who led them astray, they called down (a curse) upon their masters.

﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾: a double portion of punishment for their own straying, and a double portion for leading astray those whom they led astray. Al-Jumhur read (kathīran), with the thāʾ (ث). Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿraj, according to one report from him, read it with the bāʾ (ب), i.e., (kabīran), "great."

﴿Like those who harmed Moses﴾. It was said: this was revealed concerning the affair of Zayd and Zaynab, and what was heard about it from some people's talk. It was also said: what is meant is the story of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk), on the basis that no prophet was harmed as you were harmed. In the hadith of the man who said about a division that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had made: "This is a division by which the face of God was not sought," and became angry and said: "May God have mercy on my brother Moses; he was harmed more than this and was patient." The harming of Moses consisted of their saying that he had a skin disease (abraṣ) and a swelling of the testicles (ādar), and that he envied his brother Hārūn and killed him. Or it is the story of the hired prostitute who was to claim that Moses had committed fornication with her. Or it is what they attributed to him of sorcery and madness. These are the opinions.

﴿From what they said﴾: that is, from the accusation (wasm) of what they said. (Mā), "what," may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya).

﴿And he was honored in the sight of God﴾. Al-Jumhur read (ʿinda Allāh) with the adverbial phrase governing (wajīhan), meaning: having standing and rank before God, the Exalted, who removes harm from him and repels accusations. ʿAbd Allāh, al-Aʿmash, and Abū Ḥaywa read (ʿabdun), from servitude (ʿubūdiyya), with the (lām) of the preposition (lillāh) in the genitive, and (ʿabdan) as the predicate of (kāna), and (wajīhan) as its attribute. Ibn Khālawayh said: I prayed behind Ibn Shanabūdh in the month of Ramadan, and I heard him recite: (wa kāna ʿabdu Allāh), in accordance with the reading of Ibn Masʿūd.

Ibn Zayd said: (wajīhan) means accepted. Al-Ḥasan said: one whose supplication is answered; he asked for nothing except that he was given it, except seeing God in this world. Quṭrub said: of high rank. It was also said: his standing was that God spoke to him and gave him the title Kalīm Allāh, "the one who spoke with God."

The word (sadīd) has already been explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: here it means correct (ṣawāb). Muqātil and Qatāda said: upright (sadīdan) concerning the affair of Zayd, Zaynab, and the Messenger. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima also said: "There is no god but God." It was said: what its outward meaning agrees with its inward meaning. It was said: it is correction, from straightening the arrow so that it hits the target. It was also said: (sadīd) includes all good things.

Righteous deeds and the forgiveness of sins are made to follow from the upright word. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this verse confirms the one before it. That one was built upon the prohibition against what harms the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this one upon the command to fear God in guarding the tongue, so that prohibition and command follow one another upon them. The prohibition is followed by what contains a warning, in the story of Moses, and the command is followed by a far-reaching promise. Thus the restraint against harm and the motive to abandon it become stronger. End. It is a fine statement.

[p. 250] It was the custom of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) that free women and slave women would go out with their faces uncovered, wearing a shift (dir') and a headcover (khimar). Adulterers would accost them when they went out at night to attend to their needs among the palm groves and the thickets, mistaking them for slave women. Sometimes they would accost a free woman on the pretext that she was a slave, saying, "We thought she was a slave." So they were commanded to differ in their dress from the dress of slave women, by wearing outer garments (ardiyah) and wraps (malahif) and by covering their heads and faces, so that they would be modest and be respected, and so that no one would have designs on them. It is also related that in Medina there were people who would sit on the mounds (su'udat) to look at women, to confront them and to solicit them, and so this verse was revealed.

It has been said: the jalabib are the outer garments that cover from above down to the bottom. Ibn Jubayr said: they are the veils (maqani'). It has also been said: they are the wraps (malahif). It has been said: the jilbab is every garment a woman wears over her other clothes. It has also been said: it is anything with which one covers oneself, of cloth or otherwise. Abu Zayd said:

"I wrapped myself in a jilbab of the blackness of night."

It has been said: the jilbab is larger than the khimar. Ikrimah said: she casts a side of the jilbab over the rest of her body, so that it is not seen. 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, when asked about this, said: that she places her outer garment above her eyebrow, then turns it around until she places it over her nose. al-Suddi said: she covers one of her eyes, her forehead, and the other side [of her face] except the eye. End of the quotation. This is also the custom in the lands of al-Andalus: nothing of the woman appears except one of her eyes. al-Kisa'i said: they should cover themselves with their wraps, drawn tight over them, meaning by "drawing tight" the sense of "bringing near" (idna'). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: this is that she winds it over the forehead and fastens it, then folds it over the nose; and even if her eyes show, it still covers the chest and most of the face.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿ونِساءِ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and the women of the believers") include both free women and slave women. The temptation regarding slave women is greater, because of how much they move about freely, unlike free women; so excluding them from the general term "women" requires a clear proof. The "min" in ﴿مِن جَلابِيبِهِنَّ﴾ ("some of their jalabib") is partitive (lil-tab'id). And ('alayhinna) "over them" covers their entire bodies, or ('alayhinna) "over them" refers to their faces, because what used to show of them in the Jahiliyyah was the face.

﴿ذَلِكَ أدْنى أنْ يُعْرَفْنَ﴾ ("That is more suitable that they be recognized") — by their chastity, by their covering, so that they are not accosted and are not addressed with what they dislike. For when a woman is in the utmost state of covering and drawing close, no one approaches her, unlike a woman who displays herself, who is open to solicitation. (وكانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا) ("and God is ever Forgiving, Merciful") is an encouragement to women to leave off covering before they were commanded to do so.

When He mentioned the state of the polytheist who harms God and His Messenger, and the openly hostile one who harms the believers, He mentioned the state of the secret one who harms God and His Messenger, while displaying the truth and concealing hypocrisy. Since those who cause harm are three, in terms of the harm they do to God, His Messenger, and the believers, the polytheists are also three: a hypocrite, one in whose heart is a disease, and a rumor-monger (murjif). The hypocrite harms in secret; the second harms the believer by pursuing his women; and the third spreads rumors about the Messenger, saying: "He has been defeated, he will be expelled from Medina, he will be seized, his expeditions have been routed." The apparent sense of the conjunction is difference by individual, so the meaning would be: "If the hypocrites do not desist from their enmity and their scheming, and the debauched from their wickedness, and the rumor-mongers from what they say of the reports of evil [lit. "news of evil"] which they spread," (p. 251) "it may also be that the difference is by attribute, so that it is one person with three attributes." Just as it came: "Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women," and He mentioned ten attributes, while the one described by them is one [group]. He specified these two attributes of the hypocrites because of how severe their harm to the believers is.

Ikrimah said: (الَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ) ("those in whose hearts is a disease") is amorousness and love of fornication, and from it is: ﴿فَيَطْمَعَ الَّذِي في قَلْبِهِ مَرَضٌ﴾ ("so that one in whose heart is a disease might be tempted") [al-Ahzab: 32]. al-Suddi said: the disease is hypocrisy, and "those in whose hearts is a disease." Ibn 'Abbas said: they are those who harmed 'Umar. al-Kalbi said: those who harm the Muslims. Ibn 'Abbas said: (المُرْجِفُونَ) ("the rumor-mongers") are those who seek out discord. Qatadah said: those who harm the hearts of the believers by suggesting killing and defeat.

﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ بِهِمْ﴾ ("We will surely set you against them") means: We will empower you over them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: We will surely guard you through them.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ فِيها﴾ ("then they will not remain your neighbors in it") means: in Medina. ﴿ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ﴾. The conjunction was not with "fa" (then/so) because He did not intend that it be a consequence of the incitement; rather, its being the answer to the oath is more eloquent. The conjunction was with "thumma" (then), because expulsion from the homeland was greater for them than everything else they were afflicted with, so the state of expulsion is separated in time from the state of incitement. (إلّا قَلِيلًا) ("except for a little") means: a little neighborliness, or a little time, or a small number. This last is an exception from the spoken [subject], namely the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾; or qalilan is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), meaning: except as a few. The first is an exception from the verbal noun (masdar) indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾, and the second is from the time indicated by ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. The meaning is that they will be compelled to seek expulsion from Medina for fear of being killed.

﴿مَلْعُونِينَ﴾ ("cursed") is in the accusative as a form of blame (dhamm), as al-Tabari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it could be a substitute (badal) for (قَلِيلًا) "a little." He said: it is from the exception (iqla') which we have assumed. He also allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾. He said: it is as if he said: "they will be expelled from the city, cursed," and so one does not estimate ﴿لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ﴾ but estimates "they will be expelled" — this is good.
